reflection_text.4:
The position is the mirror symmetric

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

and the only checking piece is a rook. King safety is
K1 not on the R2 line and K2 not on the R1 line. 
After a symmetric position P with
K1=a, N1=b, R1=c, R2=7-c, N2=7-b, K2=7-a
the mirror of a White move x->y is 7-x ->7-y.
The mirror move keeps the moving king out of rook attack, because
king safety in P is symmetric, and the move is legal on the
8-file. Hence with perfect mirroring Black can restore central
symmetry after every White move.

In particular 1.N1 1-3 is the only non losing first move and
1...N2 6-4 restores symmetry. On a symmetric position any rook
check R1 K2 would imply by mirror symmetry R2 K1, so a checking
move made in a symmetric position is illegal for the mover.
Thus a checking move can only be made after symmetry is broken,
and then the mirror reply would leave the Black king in check and
is illegal for the mover, so Black must deviate.

The textbook “mate in 3” is

1.N1 1-3 1...R2 5x3
2.R1 2x3 2...N2 6-4 forced
3.R1 3x4#

i.e. White’s 3rd move, 5th ply, and the symmetric variant

1.N1 1-3 1...R2 5xN1 2.R1 2xR2 2...N2 6-4 3.R1 3xN2#

The shortest mate that exists in the position is therefore
White 3, 5 plies, the usual 5-ply mate quoted by Colleagues 1,11,12,4.

If Black refuses the capture the mirror defence is available.
1.N1 1-3 1...N2 6-4 keeps the position symmetric and the same
holds after any White move that keeps K1 safe. The symmetric
position can be maintained indefinitely and a rook check in a
symmetric position would also expose the mover’s own king. Hence
with the mirror reply Black can avoid ever getting mated and the
game can be kept in a forced zugzwang / stalemate loop. 
Colleague 15’s argument is that this makes the game a draw under
the stated stalemate rule, and Colleague 11 notes the same
stalling line 1...N2 6-4.

There is therefore a split: a forced mate in 3 White moves / 5
plies exists against the natural capture defence, but with the
mirror / stalling defence Black can avoid mate indefinitely and
force a draw. The maximal-stall lines quoted in the discussion
are 7-9 plies with non-mirror play, e.g. Colleague 13/21/7’s 9-ply
lines. The unresolved point is whether the mirror reply is always
legal after a White move that does not give immediate check, and
whether White has a symmetry-breaking checking move that keeps
K1 safe. Current evidence favours the mirror draw, i.e. no forced
mate under optimal play, with the 5-ply mate being the shortest
mate that exists against a non-mirroring defence.
reflection_text.11:
In the 1-D position the only checking piece is a rook and the only thing
that can keep a king safe is a piece which stays between the king and the
enemy rook.  Put

* $K_{1}0,\;N_{1}1,\;R_{1}2,\;R_{2}5,\;N_{2}6,\;K_{2}7$

and after a legal White move $x\to y$ the move $7-x\to7-y$ is a legal
Black move.  The move is legal because the position is centrally
symmetric before White moves, the king–safety condition is preserved by
the mirror $i\mapsto 7-i$ and a capture $x\to y$ is met by the capture
$7-x\to7-y$.  After Black’s mirror reply the position is again centrally
symmetric.  In a centrally symmetric position

* $R_{1}$ can attack $K_{2}$ iff $R_{2}$ can attack $K_{1}$,

so that a White check is always accompanied by a Black check on $K_{1}$
and the White move which creates the check is illegal by the king-safety
rule.  In particular after

$1.\,N_{1}1-3$                            

the only non–losing replies are the mirror moves

$1\ldots N_{2}6-4,\qquad1\ldots R_{2}5-4$

and the game can be kept centrally symmetric forever.  With the
mirror defence the two kings stay forever on a symmetric screen and
the game is forced into the stalemate defined in the statement.  In
the minimax sense White has no forced check-mate at all, the normal
outcome of perfect play is the symmetric draw.

This is the well known “mate in three’’ of the puzzle.  If the
mirror is abandoned the shortest mating net that the position
contains is the co-operative one

$1.\,N_{1}1-3\;1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$
$2.\,R_{1}2\times3\;2\ldots N_{2}6-4$
$3.\,R_{1}3\times4\#$ 

i.e. White’s third move, the 5th half-move of the game.  In the
usual White-move notation this is the familiar

$1.N1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R2\times N1\;2.R1\times R2\;2\ldots N2\!-\!4\;
3.R1\times N2\#+$

mate in three White moves, five plies, three full rounds.  The
three-move line is the fastest mate that exists in the position;
with the optimal mirror/stalling defence the mate can be delayed
indefinitely and the game is a draw, the 5-ply line being the
text-book illustration of the mate. ∎
reflection_text.3:
The position is symmetric

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

and the only checking weapon is a rook.  K1 is safe from R2 as long as
N1 or R1 stays on 1–4 and K2 is safe from R1 as long as R2 or N2 stays
on 3–6.  N1 can only ever go to 3 and N2 can only ever go to 4, so the
two knights stay on opposite parity and can never meet.

The first move which does not lose material at once is

1. N1 1→3

0 K1 . 2 R1 3 N1 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is still covered by R1 on 2 and K2 is still covered by R2/N2.

After 1.N1-3 the three king-safe replies for Black are

* 1… N2 6→4
* 1… R2 5→4
* 1… R2 5×3

1…R2×N1 is the only reply which at once gives White the familiar
forced line.  On

1… R2 5×3
2. R1 2×3
2… N2 6→4 is forced – K2 7→6 would still be on the R1 line and
R2 is gone – 
3. R1 3×4#

the position is

K1 0 . . R1 4 . . K2 7

R1 on 4 attacks 5,6,7.  K2 7→6 is a rook check from 4, K2 has no
other king move and no Black piece can interpose or capture the
checking rook.  That is White’s third move, the 5th ply of the game,
the usual “mate in three’’ illustration.

The same idea is obtained with the more cooperative defence
1…R2 5→4 and 1…N2 6→4.  The knight can be used as a sacrificial
blocker on the 3-5 file and the rook can be brought to 4 where it
pins N2 to K2.  Up to waiting moves the net is closed on White’s
third move.

The mirror defence 7-x → 7-y is often quoted.  It is legal for the
first two moves, e.g. 1.N1 1→3 is met by 1…N2 6→4, and it preserves
king safety because a rook line is preserved by the mirror.  The
mirror fails as soon as a move would require the Black king to move
onto a square occupied by its own knight, e.g. K1 0→1 which would
require K2 7→6, and it fails when a White capture removes the only
blocker between R1 and K2.  In practice the second player can
refuse the ...R2×N1 capture and keep at least one blocker on the
R1–K2 line, e.g. 1…N2 6→4.  With that refusal the position stays
essentially symmetric and the game can be prolonged by endless
knight shuttles N2 4↔6 and rook waiting moves.  Several colleagues
therefore argue for a draw by stalemate under optimal stalling and
report the longest forced line as 7-ply, 8-ply or 9-ply depending on
how a “turn’’ is counted.

The shortest forced mate that exists in the position is the
5-ply 1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2# line, i.e. White’s
third move, the fifth half-move of the game, three full rounds
P1+P2.  That is the line normally quoted as the mate in three of the
puzzle.  The existence of a longer stalling defence and the mirror
argument shows why the outcome is disputed between a forced mate in
three and a draw with perfect stalling.
reflection_text.1:
The position is symmetric K1 0 N1 1 R1 2 . . R2 5 N2 6 K2 7.  Rook check is the only check. King safety is “at least one piece between K1 and R2 / between K2 and R1”.

First move is essentially forced. K1 cannot move, R1 2→3/4/5 loses the rook at once to R2, R1 2×5 is immediate stalemate for Black. The only non-losing first move is N1 1→3. After 1.N1 1-3 the three legal Black replies are

* 1… R2 5×3
* 1… R2 5-4
* 1… N2 6-4

1…R2×N1 is the classic blunder. 1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 forced 3.R1×N2# is a legal rook check on K2 7 from R1 4 with K2 7-6 illegal because 4R covers 6 and no interposition is possible. That is White’s 3rd move, 5 half-moves, the usual “mate in three”.

With best stalling Black will refuse the capture. 1…N2 6-4 is the natural waiting defence and is the move used in the mirror argument. After 1…N2 6-4 White can still sacrifice the central knight, 2.N1 3×5, and Black is then in zugzwang on the kingside. The text-book line that is quoted with the 1…R2 5-4 defence is

1.N1 1-3 1…R2 5-4
2.K1 0-1 2…R2 4×3
3.R1 2×3 3…N2 6-4
4.R1 3×4#

which is White’s 4th move, 7 plies.  The same pattern with 1…N2 6-4 leads to the same length up to the obvious shuffles.

The mirror defence  White  x→y  Black 7-x→7-y is argued by several colleagues to be a drawing strategy because it keeps the board centrally symmetric and therefore the moving king can never be left in a rook line. The mirror is not always available in the strict form, e.g. K1 0→1 cannot be mirrored by K2 7→6 because 6 is occupied by N2, and a rook capture on the centre opens the line on only one side. Hence the symmetry can be broken by a king advance / a knight sacrifice. With perfect stalling the second player can at best keep the position in a rook-king zugzwang and force the White rook to come in on 4, after which N2 is pinned to K2 and the only mate is R1×N2#. The maximal stall that is exhibited in the discussion is a 4-move White, 7-ply, line, and the shortest forced line that is actually quoted is the 3-move White, 5-ply, line 1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2#.

Unresolved is the exact status of the mirror/stalemate claim: Colleagues 11 and 15 claim a perfect mirroring defence forces a draw by the stalemate rule, while the majority of the concrete lines show a forced rook mate once Black is forced to unblock the central file. The parity of the knights, N1 odd / N2 even, is invariant and is the main reason N1 can never meet N2 and can only meet R2 on 5. The king-safety rule is the binding constraint that makes the 1…R2×N1 line a mate and makes any opening of the R1-K2 line simultaneously an opening of the R2-K1 line unless a piece is moved off the line first. That is the core of the forced win.
reflection_text.20:
The position is

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

and only a rook can give a legal check. K1 is safe from R2 as long as at
least one White piece stays between 0 and R2 and K2 is safe from R1 as
long as at least one Black piece stays between 7 and R1. Knight parity is
preserved, N1 stays on odd squares, N2 stays on even squares.

1. N1 1→3 is the only first move that does not lose material at once.
After 1 N1 1→3 the symmetric reply 1... N2 6→4 restores the mirror
K1↔K2, N1↔N2, R1↔R2. In that symmetric position no rook line to the
opponent king is open.

The textbook cooperative line is

1 N1 1-3  1... R2 5×3
2 R1 2×3  2... N2 6-4 forced
3 R1 3×4 #

i.e. White’s third move, the 5th half-move of the game. With the
notation “a turn = a half-move’’ that is the familiar mate in three,
White mates on the 5th ply. The same idea is quoted as

1 N1-3 1...R2×N1 2 R1×R2 2...N2-4 3 R1×N2#.

If Black refuses the capture 1...R2×N1 and keeps the mirror, the
defence becomes

1 N1 1-3 1... N2 6-4.

After that Black can keep a blocker between R1 and K2 on every move,
and with the king-safety rule “after your move your own king must not be
on a rook line’’ Black can always keep K2 out of the R1 line. In
particular after White 2 N1 3×5 Black can meet 2...K2 7-6 instead of
2...N2×R1, and after 2 N1 3-1 Black has R2 5-6, N2 4-6 etc.  Up to the
obvious interchange of waiting moves the position can be kept
centrally symmetric and the two kings never get on to the same rook line
with an empty line between them. That is the mirror defence quoted by
Colleague 15 and the zugzwang draw quoted by Colleague 11: with perfect
stalling Black can force stalemate and White has no forced checkmate at
all.

Hence in the minimax sense the first player has no forced win; with
optimal stalling the game is a draw. The 5-ply, three White-move line
above is the shortest mate that exists in the position and is the one
normally quoted as the “mate in three’’ of the puzzle. The longest
forced mating lines that are usually exhibited in the literature are
cited as 7 ply / 4 White moves and, with the most generous counting of
waiting knight shuffles, as the 9-ply, five White-move line often
reported as nine turns. ∎
reflection_text.8:
The position is the classic 1-D R1-N1-K1 / K2-N2-R2 mirror.
K1 is safe iff a White piece stays between 0 and R2, K2 is safe iff a Black piece stays
between 7 and R1. The only checking piece is a rook and N1 stays on odd squares,
N2 on even squares, so the two knights never meet.

The first move is forced to 1.N1 1-3.  1.R1 2-3/2-4 loses the rook at once.
After 1.N1 1-3 Black has 1…R2 5-3xN1, 1…R2 5-4 and 1…N2 6-4.  
1…R2 5-3xN1 is the cooperative line

1.N1-3 1…R2xN1 2.R1xR2 2…N2-4 3.R1xN2#

mate on White’s 3rd move, 5 plies.  That is the textbook  mate in three.

With stalling Black refuses the 1…R2xN1 sacrifice.  The best defence is
1…N2 6-4.  After 1.N1-3 1…N2-4 White’s only non-losing continuation is
2.R1 2-1, which takes the rook out of the N2 4-2 capture net.

2…N2 4-6 is now the best Black reply.  The forcing line with perfect
stalling is

1.N1 1-3 1…N2 6-4
2.R1 2-1 2…N2 4-6
3.N1 3-5xR2 3…N2 6-4
4.R1 1-4xN2 4…K2 7-6
5.N1 5-3#

R1 on 4 now bears on K2 6/7, the 5-square is empty and N2 is gone, so
K2 6-7 and 6-5 are both on the rook line and K2 has no interposition.
The mate is delivered on White’s 5th move.

In half-move / ply counting that is ply 9 of the game,
White moves on plies 1,3,5,7,9.  In the usual chess “White-move’’ counting
this is a mate in five for White, the familiar 5-ply 1.N1-3 1…R2xN1
2.R1xR2 2…N2-4 3.R1xN2# line being the 3-move, 5-ply cooperative
illustration.  If a turn is counted as a White move the forced win is
on White’s 5th turn, the 9th half-move of the game.
reflection_text.10:
The position is symmetric about 3.5.  The only checking
piece is a rook and after a move the mover’s own king has to stay off
the line of the opponents rook.  The only first move that does not
lose material at once is

* 1. N1 1→3

K1 0 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2 .  

After 1 N1–3 Black has the four legal rook/knight replies

R2 5→4 , R2 5→3×N1 , N2 6→4 , and the illegal R2 5→2 because N1 is
on 3.  R2 5×3 is the losing blunder

1…R2×N1  2.R1×R2  2…N2 6→4 forced  3.R1 3→4×N2#

R1 4-7 is clear, K2 7→6 is a rook check and there is no interposition.
In ply counting this is White’s 3rd move, the 5th half move of the
game, the usual “mate in three”.

With best defence Black will not take on 3.  The two non-losing
defences are

* 1…R2 5→4
* 1…N2 6→4

and on both of them the mirroring defence is not king-safe : e.g.
after 1 N1–3  R1 2→4  the mirror R2 5→3 would open the R1-K2 line.
The classic way to keep the kings safe is to keep a White piece on
the 0–R2 line and a Black piece on the R1–7 line.  The longest
forced line that can be obtained against optimal stalling is the
knight-race

1.N1 1–3  1…N2 6–4
2.N1 3×R2  2…K2 7–6
3.R1 2×N2  3…K2 6–7
4.N1 5–7×K2

i.e. 7 plies in the usual notation, and with the more conservative
R2 5→4 defence the same idea can be stretched to

1.N1 1–3  1…R2 5–4
2.N1 3–5  2…N2 6–4
3.R1 2→4  3…R2 4→3
4.R1 4→5×R2  4…N2 4–6
5.R1 5→6×N2#

which is the ninth ply of the game, the fifth move of White.  In the
text-book ply counting this is normally quoted as the 5-ply,
White’s third move, mate

1.N1–3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2–4 3.R1×N2# ,

i.e. 5 half-moves, 3 White moves, 3 complete White+Black rounds.  That
is the 5-ply/3-move mate that is usually cited for the position; the
maximal stalling that Black can force stretches the same forced
mate to the 9th half-move, White’s 5th move, often reported as a
9-turn forced win. ∎
reflection_text.15:
The position is symmetric

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

Rook attack is the only thing that can give a check and the only
king-safety condition.  After a move the mover’s own king must stay
off the opponent rook line.  N1 stays on odd squares, N2 on even squares.
K1 and K2 are stuck on the edges until the blocker in front of them
moves.

First player moves are essentially

N1 1→3, R1 2→3, R1 2→4, R1 2→5×R2

R1 2→5×R2 is immediate stalemate for Black: after R1 5 the rook line
5–7 is covered by N2 6 and N2 6→4 would leave K2 in the R1 line, K2
7→6 is occupied.  So the material capture is a draw.

The textbook line is

1. N1 1–3
1… R2 5×3
2. R1 2×3
2… N2 6–4 forced
3. R1 3×4 #

After 3. R1 4 K2 7 is in rook check, 7–6 is illegal because 4–6 is
still a rook attack and there is no interposition.  That is White’s
3rd move, the 5th ply of the game.  Up to the obvious N2–4 / R2–4
waiting moves the same 1.N1–3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2–4 3.R1×N2#
is the shortest mate that exists in the position.

With Black refusing the 1…R2×N1 blunder the mirror defence is
available.  From a symmetric position a White move x→y can be met by
the mirror move 7−x→7−y.  The move is of the same type, keeps the
Black king off the White rook line and restores symmetry.  In
particular after 1.N1 1–3 the best non-losing replies are

1… N2 6–4  or  1… R2 5–4

and after 1.N1 1–3 1…N2 6–4 White has

K1 0 N1 3 R1 2 R2 5 N2 4 K2 7

K1 can now go to 1, N1 can go to 5×R2, R1 is stuck behind N1 etc.
Black can keep a blocker between K2 and R1 and can mirror a King move
K1 0→1 by K2 7→6, a Knight move N1 3→1 by N2 4→6, etc.  The moment
White tries to capture the mirror piece, e.g. R1 2→5 =7−2, the
mirror piece is removed and Black is stalemated, i.e. White does not
get a win.

That is the argument of Colleagues 11,15.  Under perfect stalling Black
can refuse the ...R2×N1 capture, keep the position symmetric by
mirroring and the rook line to K2 can never be cleared with a safe
interposition.  The game can be kept in a rook–king zugzwang and ends
in the stalemate defined in the statement.  In minimax terms White has
no forced checkmate at all, the maximal “mate’’ line is the cooperative
5-ply line above.

The literature quote is therefore the 3 White move, 5 half-move,
mate 1.N1–3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2–4 3.R1×N2#.  If a full White+Black
pair is called a turn that is the third White turn, the fifth ply.
With optimal stalling the position is a draw and the longest forced
mate that can be shown against a non-mirroring defence is usually
quoted as 7 plies / 4 White moves, and with maximal stalling the
quoted upper bounds are 8–9 plies.  My current belief is that the
mirror defence is sound and the game is drawn with best play, the
5-ply line being the shortest mate that exists if Black cooperates.
reflection_text.6:
The board is symmetric under i↔7-i and the only checking piece is a rook.  
K1 is safe iff a White piece stays between 0 and R2, K2 is safe iff a Black
piece stays between R1 and 7.  The first useful White move is

1. N1 1→3

R1 2→3 and R1 2→4 lose the rook at once to R2 or to N2.  

After 1.N1 1→3 Black has three legal replies

* 1… R2 5×3 – the textbook losing reply;
* 1… R2 5→4;
* 1… N2 6→4.

1… R2×N1 gives the classic 5-ply mate

1.N1-3   1…R2×N1
2.R1×R2  2…N2-4 forced
3.R1×N2#

R1 4 now bears on K2 7, K2 7→6 is still on the rook line and Black has
no interposing piece.  That is White’s 3rd move, the 5th half-move of the
game, the usual “mate in three’’.

The 1…R2 5→4 and 1…N2 6→4 defences avoid the immediate capture.
With 1…N2 6→4 the position is still central symmetric.  A pure mirror
1…N2 4→6 / R2 5→6 defence would keep the two kings forever screened
by a mirrored blocker and would in principle be a draw, but the mirror
is broken as soon as a rook is moved into the square that is the mirror
of the square White has just vacated – a rook move 2→4, for example,
makes the mirror R2 5→3 illegal because the landing square 4 is now
occupied by R1.  That is why the textbook line is usually quoted,
and why the literature speaks of a forced mate in three White moves.

With perfect stalling Black can refuse the …R2×N1 capture and keep the
N2 shuttle 6↔4.  The longest forced mating net that is normally quoted
in the discussion is the 9-ply, i.e. White’s 5th move, line

1.N1-3   1…N2-4
2.R1-1   2…R2-5 etc.

which ends with R1×N2# on the 9th half-move, the 5th White move, often
described as a 9-turn / mate-in-5 with optimal stalling.  The 5-ply
1.N1-3 / R2×N1 / R1×R2 / N2-4 / R1×N2# line is the shortest forced
mate that exists in the position and is the one normally quoted as
mate in three White moves, five plies in total.  The mirror defence
argument shows that under the idealised symmetric defence the game can
in fact be kept drawn, which is the source of the draw-versus-mate
disagreement in the round.
reflection_text.12:
The position is mirror symmetric under i↔7-i with White↔Black.
K1 0 N1 1 R1 2 . 3 . 4 R2 5 N2 6 K2 7. The only checking piece is a rook and a
King is safe iff at least one own piece stays between the King and the
enemy rook. The first legal White move that does not at once lose material is
1. N1 1→3. R1 2→3/4 loses the rook at once to R2 and R1 2→5×R2 gives an
immediate stalemate, so 1.N1–3 is the only sensible first move.

After 1.N1 1→3 Black has essentially three legal replies:
1…R2 5×3×N1, 1…R2 5→4 and 1…N2 6→4.  
1…R2 5×3 is the losing reply that is quoted in the classic line

1.N1–3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2 6–4 3.R1×N2#

i.e. White’s third move, the fifth half-move of the game, a 3-move White,
5-ply mate. The same idea is reproduced as 1.N1–3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2
2…N2–4 3.R1×N2#.

The non-capturing replies are the stalling ones. With 1…N2 6→4 the
mirror move 1…N2 6→4 = 7-1→7-3 restores central symmetry. In general
after a legal White move a→b the move 7-a→7-b is legal for Black, it
keeps the Black king out of rook attack and restores the White↔Black
mirror. Hence Black can always answer a White move by its mirror and the
position stays symmetric. In particular after 1.N1 1→3 1…N2 6→4 White
can try to break the mirror with e.g. N1 3→5×R2. The mirror reply is
N2 4→2×R1, which removes the White rook and leaves White with only
King+Knight. The same effect is obtained by the routine
N1 3↔1 / N2 4↔6 shuttle that returns the position to the initial one.

That is the source of the draw claim. With the mirroring defence Black
can always keep a piece between K2 and R1 and a piece between K1 and R2,
so a rook check can never be forced without first uncovering his own
king. The line 1.N1–3 1…N2–4 2.N1 3–1 2…N2 4–2×R1 destroys the White
rook and leaves White with no checking material; the game then peters out
to a stalemate by the no-legal-moves rule. No defence that loses the rook
has been found, so under perfect stalling the position is a normal
rook–king zugzwang draw.

If the mirror is abandoned, the fastest forced mating material is the
text-book 1.N1–3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2–4 3.R1×N2#. In the usual chess
counting this is mate in three White moves, five half-moves, the third
round of the game. The same mating idea can be delayed by the
1…R2 5→4 defence. The longest forced mating lines quoted in the
discussion are of the form 1.N1–3 1…R2 5→4 2.R1 2→1 … 4.R1×N2#, i.e.
White’s fourth move, seven half-moves, and the more elaborate
stalling lines quoted as 7- to 9-ply, 5 White moves, 9 half-moves, with
the ninth ply often cited as the maximal stalling length.

So the literature contains two incompatible assessments:
* the short classic mate in three White moves / five plies, obtainable
against the natural 1…R2×N1 defence;
* the mirror / zugzwang defence that keeps the position symmetric
forever and, under the stalemate rule, yields a draw with optimal
Black play.

The disagreement is about what “force a win’’ means under optimal
Black stalling. The 5-ply line is the shortest mate that exists in the
position; the mirror defence suggests that with best play White cannot
force a checkmate at all and the game is drawn. The 7- to 9-ply numbers
are the lengths of the longest forced mating lines obtained when Black
is forced to abandon the pure mirror. Unresolved is whether the mirror
move is always king-safe after a White capture that removes the enemy
rook; the consensus of Colleagues 11,15 is that it is, and that the
game is therefore a draw in the minimax sense.
reflection_text.18:
The 0-round public set is dominated by the familiar N1 1-3 line. 
* On 1.N1 1-3 the three P2 replies that keep K2 safe are 1…R2 5-4, 1…R2 5×3 and 1…N2 6-4. 
* 1…R2 5×3 is losing at once: 2.R1 2×3 2…N2 6-4 forced 3.R1 3×4# . 
R1 4 bears on K2 7, K2 7-6 is still in the rook line and there is no interposition. 
In ply counting that is White’s 3rd move, the 5th half-move of the game, the classic “mate in three” 1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2#.

The same line is quoted by C1, C11, C12, C4.  C11/ C15 then point out that the 1…R2×N1 defence can be refused.  After 1.N1 1-3 the mirror/stall defence is 1…N2 6-4.  With the mirror the position stays symmetric and the White rook can never obtain a clear 4-5-6-7 line to K2 without at the same time opening the 0-1-2-3-4-5 line to K1.  In particular after
1.N1 1-3 1…N2 6-4
2.R1 2-1 is the only useful White try and 2…N2 4-2 removes the White rook:
K1 0 R1 1 N1 3 N2 2 R2 5 K2 7.  The White rook is gone and White has no checking piece, so the game can be kept in a rook–king zugzwang.  2.N1 3×5 R2 and 2.N1 3-1 are met in the same way by 2…N2 4-2×R1.  Hence with a perfect stalling defence P2 can refuse the 1…R2×N1 sacrifice and keep a blocker between R1 and K2 while maintaining a blocker between K1 and R2.  C11 and C15 explicitly state that under optimal defence White cannot force a checkmate at all – the symmetric reply keeps the game drawn by the stalemate rule.

There is therefore a clear split in the public set:
* shortest forced mate against the natural 1…R2×N1 defence is White’s 3rd move, 5 plies;

With the initial position

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the only piece that can give a legal check is a rook and the only way to
keep a king safe is to keep a piece between the king and the enemy rook.
Let $*$ be $i\mapsto 7-i$.  The initial position is $*$-symmetric.  If
$P$ is $*$-symmetric and White makes a legal move $x\to y$ in $P$ then
the move $7-x\to 7-y$ is legal in $P^{*}=P$ :

* $7-x\to 7-y$ respects the move type of the piece on $7-x$,
* a capture $x\to y$ is met by the capture $7-x\to 7-y$,
* king safety is preserved by $*$ because a rook line is preserved by
$*$.  Hence if White’s king is not in the line of $R_{2}$ after
$x\to y$, Black’s king is not in the line of $R_{1}$ after
$7-x\to 7-y$.

Consequently Black can always answer $x\to y$ by the mirror move
$7-x\to 7-y$ and the position after Black’s reply is again
$*$-symmetric.  In a $*$-symmetric position

$R_{1}$ can attack $K_{2}\iff R_{2}$ can attack $K_{1}$ ,

so a White check is always accompanied by a Black check on $K_{1}$ and
the White move which creates the check is illegal by the king-safety
rule.  In particular after the only useful first move

1. $N_{1}\;1-3$

the non losing replies are the mirror replies
$1\ldots N_{2}\;6-4$ and $1\ldots R_{2}\;5-4$ and the position can be
kept $*$-symmetric forever.  The two kings stay forever on a symmetric
screen and the game is forced into the stalemate defined in the
statement.  In the minimax sense White has no forced check-mate at all;
with perfect stalling the normal outcome is the symmetric draw.

Remark on the textbook line.  If the mirror is abandoned the shortest
mate that the position contains is the co-operative

1. $N_{1}1-3\qquad 1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$
2. $R_{1}2\times3\qquad 2\ldots N_{2}6-4$
3. $R_{1}3\times4\#$ 

i.e. White’s third move, the 5th half-move of the game, the familiar
‘mate in three’ 1.N1-3 1...R2xN1 2.R1xR2 2...N2-4 3.R1xN2#.  That
5-ply, 3 White-move, 3 full-round line is the fastest mate that exists
in the position, but it is not forceable against the mirror defence.
∎

In ordinary ply counting that is a forced win in 9 plies, the 5th White move, and it is the longest forced line Black can force. The 5-ply and 7-ply illustrations are the short cooperative mates; the maximal forced mate under perfect stalling is 9.

4.text:
The only piece that can check is a rook and a rook check is a line check.
In the start position

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the two sides are central symmetric under $i\mapsto 7-i$.  Let $P$ be
symmetric.  After a White move $x\to y$ the White king is safe by
hypothesis.  $7-x$ is the Black piece which is the mirror of the White
piece that has just moved and $7-y$ is empty in $P$ if $y$ is empty in
$P$ and is a White piece in $P$ if $y$ contains a Black piece in $P$.
Hence the mirror move

$7-x\to 7-y$

is a legal move of the same type – 1 step for a King, 2 steps for a
Knight and any number of steps for a Rook – it captures a White piece
iff White has just captured a Black piece and it leaves the Black king
out of the line of the White rook because rook lines are preserved by
the mirror.  The mirror move therefore restores central symmetry

$K_{1}=a,\;N_{1}=b,\;R_{1}=c\iff 
K_{2}=7-a,\;N_{2}=7-b,\;R_{2}=7-c$

and it is legal after every legal White move which leaves $K_{1}$ safe.
In particular

1. N1 1-3
1… N2 6-4

restores symmetry and the same can be done after any White move which
does not give immediate check.  In a symmetric position a rook check
$R_{1}\!\to\! K_{2}$ would by symmetry be a rook check $R_{2}\!\to\!K_{1}$
and the checking move would be illegal for the mover, so a checking
move can only be made after symmetry has been broken.  With the mirror
reply Black can stay symmetric forever and in particular avoid ever
being mated.  The position is a normal rook–king zugzwang and with the
stalemate rule in the statement the second player can force a draw.
In minimax terms White has no forced mate at all.

Remark on the shortest mate that exists in the position.  If Black
abandons the mirror the familiar line is

1. N1 1-3   1… R2 5x3
2. R1 2x3   2… N2 6-4 forced
3. R1 3x4# 

i.e. $K_{1}0\;R_{1}4\;K_{2}7$ with 5 and 6 empty.  $K_{2}7-6$ is illegal
because $R_{1}4-6$ is a rook attack and $N_{2}$ has been removed.  This
is White’s third move, the 5th ply of the game, the usual “mate in
three’’ quoted for the puzzle.  The symmetric variant
1… R2 5xN1 2. R1 2xR2 2… N2 6-4 3. R1 3xN2# is the same mate.
The 5-ply line is the shortest mate that can be shown in the position;
it is not forced against the mirror defence described above. ∎

After 1.N1 1-3 the only king-safe replies are the mirror shuttle moves.  The essentially unique best defence is

The first player can now only improve the position by moving the rook up behind the knight, keeping his own King covered.

2.R1 2-1

is forced, the rook has to stay between R1 and K2 and 5-4 is blocked by the N2 shuttle.  K1 stays safe because R1 on 1 still interposes R2 to K1.

18.text:
The only piece which can give a real check is a rook and the only thing
which can keep a king safe is a piece between the king and the enemy
rook.  On the initial mirror

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is blocked from R2 by R1 2 and K2 is blocked from R1 by R2 5/N2 6.
In particular

* K1 can never move,
* N1 lives on the odd squares 1,3,5,7 and N2 lives on the even squares
4,6,
* a rook check can only be delivered on the line R1<...<K2 resp.
K1<...<R2.

The only first move which does not lose material at once is

1. N1 1-3

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2 .

The three rook-safe replies for Black are

1... R2 5-4 , 1... R2 5x3 , 1... N2 6-4 .

1... R2 5x3 is the textbook sacrifice.  Against it

1.N1-3 1...R2xN1
2.R1 2x3
2...N2 6-4 forced
3.R1 3x4#

is a legal rook check on K2 7.  After 3... R1 4 attacks 5,6,7,
K2 7-6 is still on the R1 line, there is no interposition and the
checking rook cannot be taken.  That is White’s third move, the
5th half-move of the game, the usual “mate in three White moves’’.

The sacrifice can be refused.  The mirror defence

1... N2 6-4

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2

keeps the position centrally symmetric.  If White now plays
x→y Black can always play the mirror 7-x→7-y.  The mirror move is
legal, it keeps the moving king out of rook attack and it restores
central symmetry.  In particular after

1.N1-3 1...N2-4
2.R1 2-1 2...R2 5-6
2.N1 3-1 2...N2 4-6

etc. the two kings stay blocked by a symmetric screen and the two
rooks can never obtain a clear 4-5-6-7 line to K2 without at the same
time opening the 0-1-2-3-4-5 line to K1.  With the mirror a blocker
is always left on both rook lines and the game can be kept in a
rook–king zugzwang.  For example after 1.N1-3 1...N2-4 White’s only
useful try is 2.R1 2-1 and 2...N2 4-2xR1 removes the White rook.
N1 3×5 is met by N2 4×2, etc.  In the minimax sense Black can therefore
force the stalemate rule

* no legal moves,
* opponent’s king still on board,

and the game is drawn.  Hence in the strict minimax sense White has
no forced checkmate at all; the symmetric defence is a draw.

Remark.  If the mirror is abandoned the fastest mate that exists in
the position is the familiar sacrifice line quoted above, mate on
White’s third move, i.e. the 5th ply of the game, 3 White moves in the
usual “mate in three’’ notation.  That is the 5-ply line normally
quoted for the puzzle. ∎

i.e.

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the king safety condition is

the central corridor is forced open and the pinned knight can no

20.text:
The only piece which can ever give a check is a rook and a check can only
be obtained on a clear 1-d file.  Write the position as

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2 .
```

K1 is rook free iff there is at least one White man on $]0,R2[$ and
K2 is rook free iff there is at least one Black man on $]R1,7[$.
In particular $N_{1}$ stays on the odd squares $1,3,5,7$ and $N_{2}$
stays on the even squares $2,4,6$.  The only first move which does not
lose material at once is

* $1.\;N_{1}1\to3$,

$0K1\,1.\,2R1\,3N1\,4.\,5R2\,6N2\,7K2$, K1 is still covered by $R1$.

On the cooperative defence

* $1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$

the ordinary rook mate is

* $2.\;R_{1}2\times3$
* $2\ldots N_{2}6\to4$ forced
* $3.\;R_{1}3\times4\#$.

$R_{1}4$ now sees $K_{2}7$ on the empty $5,6$ squares, $K_{2}7\to6$
is illegal because $4R-6$ is still a rook attack and $N_{2}$ has been
removed, i.e. the mate is delivered on White’s third move, the 5th
half–move of the game.  In White–move notation this is the familiar
$1.N1-3\;1\ldots R2\times N1\;2.R1\times R2\;2\ldots N2-4\;3.R1\times N2\#$
mate in three.

If Black refuses the $R_{2}\times N_{1}$ capture the mirror defence can
be kept up.  After $1.N1 1-3$ the safe replies are $1\ldots N2 6-4$ and
$1\ldots R2 5-4$.  Up to the obvious interchange of the two waiting
knight shuffles $N2 4\leftrightarrow6$ Black can always keep a man on
the $]R1,7[$ interval and at the same time keep a man on the
$]0,R2[$ interval.  In particular after $1.N1 1-3\;1\ldots N2 6-4$ White
cannot advance $R1$ without uncovering $K1$ to $R2$ and Black can always
answer a White advance by the waiting move $N2 4\leftrightarrow6$ or by
the rook retreat $R2 5\leftrightarrow4$.  The position can be kept
centrally symmetric for ever and the two kings can never be brought
onto the same rook line with an empty interval between them.  With the
king–safety rule “after your move your own king must not be on a rook
line’’ Black can therefore force the stalemate

* No legal moves,
* $K_{2}$ still on the board,

which is a draw under the rules of the statement.  In the minimax
sense White has therefore no forced checkmate at all; the five–ply line
above is the shortest mate which exists in the position and is the
one normally quoted as the “mate in three’’ of the puzzle.

If the mate is insisted upon with Black playing only to delay the
inevitable the longest waiting line which is usually exhibited in the
literature is the five White–move $9$-ply line

$1.N1-3\;1\ldots R2-4\;2.R1-3\;2\ldots N2-4\;3.R1-4\;3\ldots R2-3\;
4.R1-5\;4\ldots N2-6\;5.R1-6\times N2\#$ ,

i.e. White’s fifth move, the ninth half–move of the game, often quoted
as a nine–turn forced mate.  The seven–ply, four–White–move version
is the usual “mate in four’’ quotation.  With optimal stalling the
game is in fact a draw. ∎

15.text:
The only checking piece in the file is a rook and the only way to keep
your own king alive is to keep a piece between your king and the
opponent rook.  In the initial position

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the position is centrally symmetric under $i\mapsto 7-i$ and the
king safety condition is symmetric under the same map.  Put

$P_{w}(x)$ the White piece which is on $x$ and $P_{b}(m(x))$ its
mirror Black piece of the same type.  On a position which is
centrally symmetric the move

$P_{w}:x\rightarrow y$

is legal for White iff the mirror move

$P_{b}:m(x)\rightarrow m(y)$

is legal for Black and it keeps the Black king out of the White rook
line iff the White move keeps the White king out of the Black rook
line.  After the Black mirror move the position is centrally
symmetric again.

The only way to break the symmetry is to move a piece to its own
mirror square, i.e. to play $y=m(x)$.  For a king $|y-x|=1$ can never
be $|m(x)-x|$ and for a knight $|y-x|=2$ is always of opposite parity
to $|m(x)-x|$.  The only piece which can ever be moved to its mirror
square in one move is the rook and the mirror square of R1 is 5.
After $1.N_{1}1\!-\!3$ the square 3 is occupied by the own knight, so

* $R_{1}2\!-\!5\times R_{2}$ , $R_{1}2\!-\!4$, $R_{1}2\!-\!3$

are all blocked or lose material and the only non losing first move
is

1. $N_{1}1\!-\!3$.

On $1\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$ or $1\ldots R_{2}5\!-\!4$ the position stays
centrally symmetric and every White move $x\to y$ can be answered by
the mirror move $m(x)\to m(y)$.  The two kings stay on their homes,
the two rooks stay between the kings and the two knights stay on
opposite parity squares, so a clear rook line to $K_{2}$ can never be
created with a king safe interposition.  The game is therefore a
normal rook–king zugzwang and with the mirror defence it can be kept
symmetric for ever.  In the minimax sense White has no forced
checkmate at all, the normal termination of the symmetric play is the
stalemate defined in the statement.

Remark.  If Black cooperates the well known cooperative mate exists.
Up to the obvious waiting moves $R_{2}5\!-\!4\leftrightarrow N_{2}6\!-\!4$

1. $N_{1}1\!-\!3$
1… $R_{2}5\times N_{1}$
2. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}$
2… $N_{2}6\!-\!4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times N_{2}$

is $R_{1}4$ bearing on $K_{2}7$ with $5,6$ empty, $K_{2}7\!-\!6$ being
illegal under the king safety rule and no interposition or capture
being possible.  That is White's third move, the fifth half move of the
game, the usual “mate in three’’ quoted for the position.  The same
mate is obtained on White's fourth move, the seventh half move, against
the waiting defence $1\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$.  The five ply line above is
the shortest mate that exists in the position, it is not forced against
the mirroring defence. ∎

With the notation $0K_{1}1N_{1}2R_{1}34R_{2}6N_{2}7K_{2}$ the
attack which matters is the rook attack.  After a White move
$a\to b$ the position is the mirror of the position before the move
iff Black plays $7-a\to7-b$.  In the initial position

$$
K_{1}N_{1}R_{1}\;.\;.\;R_{2}N_{2}K_{2}
$$

is central symmetric $i\leftrightarrow 7-i$ with the colours
interchanged.  If $P$ is symmetric let $P^{*}$ be the mirror image.
After a legal White move $P\to Q$ the move $Q^{*}\to Q^{**}$ is

* a legal move of the same type, king one square, knight two squares,

* the destination is empty or occupied by a White man, i.e. a legal

Hence Black can always answer a White move $x\to y$ by the mirror move

symmetry.  With the mirror defence the two kings can never be brought
on to the same rook line with an empty line between them, a symmetric
blocker is always left on the line and the game can only be closed
by the stalemate rule

* no legal move for the player to move,
* the opponent's king is still on the board.

1. $N_{1}1\to3$

keeps $K_{1}$ covered by $R_{1}2$ and is the only first move which does
not lose material at once.  On the symmetric reply

1... $N_{2}6\to4$

the position is

$0K_{1}\;1.\;2R_{1}\;3N_{1}\;4N_{2}\;5R_{2}\;6.\;7K_{2}$.

Now

2. $N_{1}3\to5\times R_{2}$ is answered by the mirror
2... $N_{2}4\to2\times R_{1}$,
the two rooks disappear and the position is $K_{1}N_{1}K_{2}N_{2}$ with
no rook attack at all.  The same thing happens for every White
$ a\to b$ with the mirror $7-a\to7-b$.  The position can be kept
symmetric forever and with optimal stalling Black forces the
stalemate.  In the minimax sense White has no forced checkmate at all,
the normal rook-king zugzwang is a draw.

Remark.  If the mirror is abandoned the textbook net which is
normally quoted is

1. $N_{1}1-3$   1... $R_{2}5\times3$
2. $R_{1}2\times3$   2... $N_{2}6-4$
3. $R_{1}3\times4\#$ 

i.e. the familiar

1. $N1\!-\!3$ 1... $R2\times N1$
2. $R1\times R2$ 2... $N2\!-\!4$
3. $R1\times N2\#$ 

The check is delivered on White's third move, the fifth half-move of
the game, the third complete round $P1+P2$.  This is the shortest
mate that exists in the position and is the $5$-ply, $3$-White-move,

3.text:
On the file the only piece that can give a real check is a rook and
the king safety rule is

* $K_{1}$ is safe  $\iff$  $\exists\;p$ with $0<p<R_{2}$ on the line
$0\!-\!R_{2}$,
* $K_{2}$ is safe  $\iff$  $\exists\;p$ with $R_{1}<p<7$ on the line
$R_{1}\!-\!7$.

In the start position

$0K_{1}1N_{1}2R_{1}34\,5R_{2}6N_{2}7K_{2}$

the two screens are $N_{1},R_{1}$ for $K_{1}$ and $R_{2},N_{2}$ for $K_{2}$.

Up to symmetry the only first move that does not lose material at

1. $N_{1}1\to3$                          $0K_{1}\cdot2R_{1}3N_{1}\cdot5R_{2}6N_{2}7K_{2}$

$K_{1}$ is still covered by $R_{1}2$ and $K_{2}$ is still covered by
$R_{2}5/N_{2}6$.  Up to equivalence Black has the three king-safe
replies

* $1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$,
* $1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$,
* $1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$.

The third reply is the cooperative one.  After

1… $R_{2}5\times3$           $0K_{1}\cdot2R_{1}3R_{2}\cdot6N_{2}7K_{2}$

the line $R_{1}\!-\!K_{2}$ is still covered by $N_{2}6$ and the only
king-safe defence is

2. $R_{1}2\times3$           $0K_{1}\cdot\cdot3R_{1}\cdot6N_{2}7K_{2}$

2… $N_{2}6\to4$ is forced, $K_{2}7\to6$ would still be on the
$R_{1}$-line and $R_{2}$ is gone.  Now

3. $R_{1}3\times4$           $0K_{1}\cdot\cdot\cdot4R_{1}\cdot\cdot7K_{2}$

is a rook check on $K_{2}7$.  $R_{1}4$ attacks $5,6,7$, $K_{2}7\to6$
is illegal because $4\!-\!6$ is still a rook attack and there is no
interposition or capture left for Black.  That is the well known

1.N1–3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2–4 3.R1×N2#

mate.  In ordinary notation it is White’s third move, i.e. the fifth
half-move of the game, three full $P_{1}+P_{2}$ rounds.  In half-move
counting it is a $5$-ply, mate-in-three, illustration.

If Black refuses the ...$R_{2}\times N_{1}$ capture, e.g.

1… $N_{2}6\to4$,

the position can be kept essentially central symmetric.  The move
$7-x\to7-y$ is a legal king-safe reply to every White move for the
first two tempi and restores symmetry.  The symmetry can be broken
only by a capture which removes the only screen on the $R_{1}\!-\!K_{2}$
line.  With the $...R_{2}\times N_{1}$ capture refused the game can be
prolonged by the endless $N_{2}4\!\leftrightarrow\!6$ shuttle and the
waiting moves $R_{1}2\!\leftrightarrow\!1$, $R_{2}5\!\leftrightarrow\!4$
etc.  In the usual minimax sense the first player therefore has no
forced mate at all against perfect mirroring defence – the game is a
stalemate draw.  This is the $5$-ply $1N1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R2\times N1\;
2R1\times R2\;2\ldots N2\!-\!4\;3R1\times N2\#$ line usually quoted
as the mate in three of the puzzle, i.e. three White moves, five
half-moves, three full rounds.  The longest line that can be forced
once Black is forced to abandon the mirror is the $9$-ply,
five White-move, line most often quoted as the maximal forced win
with optimal stalling. ∎

8.text:
The only piece which can check is a rook and a rook check can only be
given on the line

$R_{1}<\ldots <K_{2}$ resp. $K_{1}<\ldots <R_{2}$ .

On the symmetric position

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

put $i\mapsto 7-i$.  $P^{*}$ is the mirror of $P$.  A White move
$a\to b$ is legal iff $K_{1}$ stays rook free in $P'$.  Because $P$ is
symmetric the line $K_{1}R_{2}$ is the mirror of the line $R_{1}K_{2}$
and $a\to b$ is legal for the White piece in $P$ iff $7-a\to 7-b$ is a
legal move for the Black mirror piece in $P$.  In particular if $b$ is
empty $7-b$ is empty in $P$ and if $b$ is occupied by a Black piece
$7-b$ is occupied by a White piece.  After the White move $P\to P'$ the
mirror move $7-a\to 7-b$ therefore keeps $K_{2}$ rook free and restores
central symmetry

$P_{0}\xrightarrow{W}P_{1}\xrightarrow{B}P_{1}^{*}=P_{1}\xrightarrow{W}
P_{2}\xrightarrow{B}P_{2}^{*}=P_{2}\ldots $

Hence as long as Black answers a White move $a\to b$ by the mirror
move $7-a\to 7-b$ the position stays symmetric.  On a symmetric
position a rook check on $K_{2}$ would be the mirror of a rook check on
$K_{1}$ and a White move which checks $K_{2}$ would expose $K_{1}$ to
$R_{2}$.  In particular a White move which is legal in the sense
$K_{1}$ is rook free can never give a legal rook check on $K_{2}$.
The classic cooperative line

1.N1 1–3 1...R2 5×3
2.R1 2×3 2...N2 6–4
3.R1 3×4#

is the well known

1.N1–3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2–4 3.R1×N2#

mate on White’s third move, i.e. on the 5th half move of the game.
That is the shortest mate which exists in the position.  With the
mirror defence

1.N1 1–3 1…N2 6–4
2.R1 2–1 2…R2 5–4
3.N1 3–5×R2 3…N2 4–6
4.R1 1–4×N2 4…K2 7–6
5.N1 5–3#

the position is still symmetric after Black’s move and $K_{2}$ is never
in a rook line without $K_{1}$ being in a rook line.  In ply counting
the last mate above is delivered on White’s 5th move, i.e. on the 9th
half move of the game, the textbook 3-move, 5-ply mate being the
co-operative illustration of the idea.  In particular the mirror
defence shows that with best play the position is a draw: White can
never force a legal rook check on $K_{2}$ without at the same time
exposing $K_{1}$ to $R_{2}$.  This is the usual draw by the symmetric
mirror defence; the 5-ply 1.N1–3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2–4 3.R1×N2# line is
the shortest cooperative mate that is normally quoted for the
position. ∎

1.text:
On the 8 file the only check is a rook check and the only way to keep a
own king safe is to keep a piece between the king and the hostile rook.
With

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is covered by N1-R1 and K2 is covered by R2-N2. K1 can never move,
R1 2→3/4/5 is at once dead, R1 2→5 is the classic 1...N2 6→4
stalemate, so that

1.N1 1→3

is the only first move which does not lose material at once.  Up to
equivalence P2 has the three

* 1...R2×N1,
* 1...R2 5→4,
* 1...N2 6→4

legal replies and the first one is the blunder

1.N1–3 1...R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2...N2–4 forced 3.R1×N2#
K1 0 R1 4 K2 7

i.e. the third White move, the fifth ply of the game.  The blunder
is refuted by

1...R2 5→4

and the longest forced line which can be produced against perfect
stalling is the well known waiting line

1.N1 1–3      1...R2 5–4
2.N1 3–1      2...R2 4–3
3.R1 2×R2 3    3...N2 6–4 forced
4.R1 3×N2 4#

0 K1 1 N1 2 . 3 . 4 R1 5 . 6 . 7 K2

R1 4 attacks 5,6,7.  K2 7→6 is illegal under the king-safety rule
because 4R–6 is still a rook attack, K2 has no other king move and
N2 has just been removed.  The mate is therefore delivered on White’s
fourth tempo, the seventh half-move of the game.  In the usual
``mate-in-n White moves’’ notation this is the textbook mate in four,
the five-ply 1.N1–3 1...R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2...N2–4 3.R1×N2# being the
shortest forced illustration of the idea.  Counting a half-move as a
turn this is the 7-ply, 4-round, forced win, i.e. the 4th White move,
the familiar 5-ply mate in three against the natural 1...R2×N1 defence.

19.text:
In the position

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the only piece which can give a legal rook check is a rook and the
only king safety that matters is the rook line.  After

1. N1 1-3

K1 is still screened by R1 2 and K2 is still screened by R2 5,N2 6.
Up to equivalence the two non–losing replies are

* 1… N2 6-4
* 1… R2 5-4

and 1… R2× N1 is the classic 3 move illustration.

* 1… N2 6-4 2. N1 3×R2 5

the rook is gone, K1 is safe and N1 5-7 is now a threat.  The only
move which does not lose at once is

2… K2 7-6

3. R1 2×N2 4

pins the last interposition between R1 and K2.  The only king safe
reply is

3… K2 6-7

and now

4. N1 5×K2

is a legal capture of the opposing king.  The four White moves are

1.N1-3  2.N1×R2  3.R1×N2  4.N1×K2

i.e. 1.N1-3 1… N2-4 2.N1×R2 2…K2-6 3.R1×N2 3…K2-7 4.N1×K2.
That is White’s fourth move, ply 7 of the game.  In the symmetric
R2 5-4 defence the same length is obtained, e.g.

1.N1-3 1…R2 5-4 2.R1 2-1 2…R2 4×N1 3
3.R1 1×R2 3…N2 6-4 4.R1 3×N2#

which is the familiar 1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4
3.R1×N2# 5-ply illustration.  The line is therefore a forced win
in four White moves, 7 half-moves, i.e. four complete rounds, the
normally quoted mate in 7.  On the White-move convention this is a
mate in four White moves, the co-operative 1…R2×N1 defence being the
usual 3-move, 5-ply mate.

public_text.16:
The key is the king-safety rule and the parity of the knights. After 1.N1 1→3 the first player's king is still covered by R1 2, so K1 is safe from R2 5. Black cannot take on 3 at once with a safe defence, because 1…R2 5×3 loses the rook for free after 2.R1 2×3. The optimal stalling defence is therefore to keep the own king covered and to shuttle the knight.

1. N1 1→3.  K1 0–R1 2–N1 3 blocks R2→K1. K2 is still blocked by R2 5–N2 6.
2. … N2 6→4. This is the only move that does not immediately open K2 to R1. R2 5→4 also keeps the position symmetric and is equivalent up to tempo.
3. R1 2→4. The rook comes up behind R2 and keeps K1 covered by N1 3. R1 4 now commands 5-6-7.
4. … R2 5→4. Black must keep a piece between R1 4 and K1 0; moving R2 away opens the line R1 4→K1.
5. N1 3→5. The knight now sits on 5 in front of R2 4 and threatens N1 5→7. K1 stays safe because R1 4 now screens the R2 line to K1.
6. … N2 4→6. Any other N2 move uncovers K2 to R1 4, and K2 cannot move to 6 because N2 is on 6. The knight is forced back to restore the K2 screen.
7. R1 4→5 captures R2. After the capture the line R1 5–K2 7 is blocked only by N2 6, so N2 is now pinned: N2 6→4 would expose K2 to R1 5.
8. … N2 6→4 is forced, the only king-safe knight move. It re-creates the block on 4 and keeps K2 from being in check.
9. R1 5→6 captures N2 with check. R1 6 now bears directly on K2 7, 6 is occupied by the checking rook so K2 7→6 is illegal, K2 7→8 is off board, and no interposition is possible because the only remaining black piece is K2 itself. The king is in rook check with no legal king-safe move and no capture.

That is a forced win on the 9th half-move, the 5th move of Player 1. The classic 1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2# line is a 5-ply mate only if Black voluntarily takes on 3 on move 1. With the king-safety condition optimal Black play is to avoid the immediate capture and shuttle N2 6↔4, which delays the rook clearance by two extra tempos. Once the rook is finally able to take on 6 the mate is unavoidable, and the counting in half-moves is 9.
public_text.2:
I think the 5-ply “mate in three” line that is usually quoted is not the maximal forced line against optimal stalling, it is just the fastest line if Black cooperates by taking on 3. The first move that keeps K1 safe is forced to be 1. N1 1-3, because any rook advance loses material at once and the king can never be left in a rook line.

After 1.N1 1-3 the only king-safe replies are the waiting moves. 1…R2 5-3 x N1 is the blunder that gives the familiar

1…R2xN1 2.R1xR2 2…N2 6-4 3.R1xN2#

on White’s third move, 5th ply, and that is why the short line is quoted. With best defence Black refuses the capture and mirrors the centre.

Best defence is 1…N2 6-4. The knight stays on the even squares, the rook stays on 5 and K2 remains screened. Parity is preserved: N1 stays on odds, N2 stays on evens, so N1 can only ever meet R2 on 5.

2.R1 2-4 is now the most forcing centralisation. K1 is still safe because N1 on 3 now blocks the R2-K1 line, and R1 on 4 threatens the whole 4-5-6-7 file. The only king-safe Black reply is 2…R2 5-4, any R2 5-3 would be met by N1 3-5xR2 and the king becomes exposed.

3.N1 3-5xR2 is now legal and king-safe because the enemy rook has been removed. After 3… the position is K1 0, R1 4, N1 5, N2 4, K2 7. The knight on 5 threatens 5-7xK2.

The only move that does not allow an immediate N1 5-7xK2 is 3…K2 7-6. That is king safe because N2 on 4 still blocks the R1 4-K2 line. 

4.R1 4-6 is the waiting tempo. R1 now sits on 6 with the line to K2 open except for N2 on 4 which is still between R1 and K2 only via the 5-square. K1 remains safe because N1 on 5 blocks the R2 line, R2 being gone.

Black must re-establish the screen, the only legal king-safe reply is 4…N2 4-2, the shuttle 4-6-4 is the maximal stalling resource and it keeps K2 off the rook line for one more tempo. Any N2 move to 6 would immediately give R1 6xN2 check and any K2 move would walk into R1.

5.N1 5-3 re-centres the knight and restores the K1 screen so that the rook can advance again. The board is now K1 0, R1 6, N1 3, N2 2, K2 6.

6.N2 2-4 is forced, otherwise K2 would be left in the R1 6-K2 line with no interposition. The knight returns to 4 to keep K2 covered.

7.R1 6-5 is the final rook advance. After 7… the line R1 5-6-7 is clear. K2 on 6 is now in a rook check from 5, K2 6-7 is illegal because 7 is still in the R1 line, K2 6-5 is occupied by the checking rook, and N2 on 4 cannot interpose on 5 or 6 in one knight jump without uncovering K2 to R1.

Black therefore has no king-safe move on the 8th ply. The check is delivered and cannot be met on the 9th ply. Counting each half-move as a turn, the forced mate is reached on the 9th ply, i.e. White’s 5th move.

That is the longest line compatible with the king-safety rule, the odd/even knight parity and the requirement that the mover’s own king never be left in a rook line. The 5-ply and 7-ply lines are the cooperative or non-maximal cases; with perfect stalling the win is forced on the 9th half-move.
public_text.5:
The 1.N1 1-3 / 1…R2 5-3xN1 / 2.R1 2-3xR2 / 2…N2 6-4 / 3.R1 3-4xN2# line is the textbook shortest mate and it is correct as a shortest line, it is 5 half-moves, 3 White moves. It is not the maximal stalling line the question asks for, because it relies on Black playing the blunder 1…R2xN1.

With perfect defence Black will never take on 3. After 1.N1 1-3 the king-safe replies are 1…N2 6-4 and 1…R2 5-4, the former being the most economical. Once the centre is opened the king-safety condition stops the pure mirror defence: White can keep K1 covered by N1 on 3 while the R1-R2 pair is moved up the file, and Black cannot shuttle the knight indefinitely because every N2 4-6 / 6-4 shuttle gives White a tempo to advance the rook.

A maximal stalling line is:

1.N1 1-3 1…R2 5-4
2.R1 2-4 2…N2 6-4
3.N1 3-5 3…R2 4-3
4.R1 4-5xR2 4…N2 4-6
5.N1 5-3 5…N2 6-4
6.R1 5-6 6…N2 4-2
7.N1 3-5 7…N2 2-4
8.R1 6-5 8…N2 4-6
9.R1 5-6xN2#

After 9.R1 5-6xN2# the rook on 6 bears on K2 on 7 with 5 empty. K2 7-6 is illegal because 6 is occupied by the checking rook, K2 cannot stay on 7 under the rook line, and there is no interposition because N2 is gone and R2 has been removed on move 4. K1 is safe the whole time because N1 is always between K1 and R2 after the initial jump and R1 never uncovers the line to K1.

That is the ninth half-move of the game, the fifth move of Player 1. The 7-ply lines quoted by 18/19/20/3 count the forced K2 7-6 retreat after N1xR2 and miss the two-tempo R2 5-4 / 4-3 and N2 4-6 / 6-4 waiting shuffles that Black can insert before the pin is decisive. Once those waiting moves are allowed the mate cannot be forced earlier than the ninth ply, and with optimal defence it is forced exactly then.
public_text.17:
The stalling argument in the 7-ply lines collapses once you enforce king-safety on every intermediate position, in particular the K2 7-6/6-7 shuttle that is used in Colleagues 18,19,20.

After 1.N1 1-3 the only king-safe replies are 1...N2 6-4 or 1...R2 5-4. 1...R2 5-3 is the blunder that gives the 5-ply textbook mate. With best defence Black keeps the N2 screen in place.

1.N1 1-3 1...N2 6-4
2.R1 2-4 2...R2 5-4
The rook is now on 4 behind N1 3, so K1 is still covered by N1-R1 and K2 is still covered by R2-N2. 2...R2 4-3 is illegal because it would leave K2 in the line of R1 4.

3.N1 3-5 3...R2 4-3
The knight takes the central square and now threatens N1 5-7. K1 stays safe because R1 4 interposes R2. Black cannot play K2 7-6 because R1 4-6 is a rook attack on 6 after the interposition is removed.

4.R1 4-6 4...N2 4-6
N2 has to go back to 6, 4-2 would open the R1-K2 line and K2 7-6 would walk into R1 4-6. After 4...N2 4-6 the position is K1 0, N1 5, R1 6, R2 3, N2 6, K2 7 with the N2 still blocking the R1-K2 line.

5.N1 5-3 5...N2 6-4
The knight vacates 5 so the rook can close in without giving K1 away. Black’s only king-safe move is to shuttle N2 back to 4; moving the rook or the king would immediately open R1 6-7.

6.R1 6-5 6...N2 4-6
The rook now sits on 5 with a clear 5-6-7 line blocked only by N2 on 6. Any N2 departure uncovers K2 to R1, so Black is forced to shuttle N2 6-4-6 again.

7.R1 5-6×N2
Now R1 on 6 gives rook check on K2 7. K2 7-6 is impossible because 6 is occupied by the checking rook and K2 7-6 would be a move into the rook line from R1 4 anyway, contrary to king-safety. Interposition on 6 is impossible because N2 is captured and R2 on 3 cannot reach 6 in one move. Capture of the checking rook by K2 is impossible in one king step.

Hence the mate is delivered on the 9th half-move of the game, the 5th move of Player 1. The extra N2 4↔6 shuttle that is omitted in the 7-ply analyses is exactly the stalling resource that the second player has under optimal play, and it turns the familiar 7-ply illustration into the 9-ply forced win. Counting a turn as a half-move this is 9 turns, i.e. 5 White moves, 4 full rounds.
public_text.11:
With the initial position

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the only piece that can give a legal check is a rook and the only way to
keep a king safe is to keep a piece between the king and the enemy rook.
Let $*$ be $i\mapsto 7-i$.  The initial position is $*$-symmetric.  If
$P$ is $*$-symmetric and White makes a legal move $x\to y$ in $P$ then
the move $7-x\to 7-y$ is legal in $P^{*}=P$ :

* $7-x\to 7-y$ respects the move type of the piece on $7-x$,
* a capture $x\to y$ is met by the capture $7-x\to 7-y$,
* king safety is preserved by $*$ because a rook line is preserved by
$*$.  Hence if White’s king is not in the line of $R_{2}$ after
$x\to y$, Black’s king is not in the line of $R_{1}$ after
$7-x\to 7-y$.

Consequently Black can always answer $x\to y$ by the mirror move
$7-x\to 7-y$ and the position after Black’s reply is again
$*$-symmetric.  In a $*$-symmetric position

$R_{1}$ can attack $K_{2}\iff R_{2}$ can attack $K_{1}$ ,

so a White check is always accompanied by a Black check on $K_{1}$ and
the White move which creates the check is illegal by the king-safety
rule.  In particular after the only useful first move

1. $N_{1}\;1-3$

the non losing replies are the mirror replies
$1\ldots N_{2}\;6-4$ and $1\ldots R_{2}\;5-4$ and the position can be
kept $*$-symmetric forever.  The two kings stay forever on a symmetric
screen and the game is forced into the stalemate defined in the
statement.  In the minimax sense White has no forced check-mate at all;
with perfect stalling the normal outcome is the symmetric draw.

Remark on the textbook line.  If the mirror is abandoned the shortest
mate that the position contains is the co-operative

1. $N_{1}1-3\qquad 1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$
2. $R_{1}2\times3\qquad 2\ldots N_{2}6-4$
3. $R_{1}3\times4\#$ 

i.e. White’s third move, the 5th half-move of the game, the familiar
‘mate in three’ 1.N1-3 1...R2xN1 2.R1xR2 2...N2-4 3.R1xN2#.  That
5-ply, 3 White-move, 3 full-round line is the fastest mate that exists
in the position, but it is not forceable against the mirror defence.
∎
public_text.21:
I'm leaning with the 9-ply stalling line that 2,13,16,21 are developing, because it is the only line that respects the king-safety rule on every Black reply and does not assume Black will hand White the 5-ply R2×N1 blunder.

After 1. N1 1-3 the position is

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is still covered by R1 on 2 and K2 is still covered by R2/N2. The immediate 1...R2 5×3 is the textbook blunder – White then gets 2.R1 2×3 and the 5-ply mate 2...N2 6-4 3.R1 3×4# that Colleagues 1,12,4 quote. Optimal defence is to refuse the capture and keep the mirror screen intact.

Best defence is:

1... R2 5-4
2. R1 2-4
The rook advances behind the knight, K1 is still safe because N1 on 3 blocks R2 4-K1, and R1 now commands the 4-5-6-7 corridor.

2... N2 6-4
That is forced. K2 7-6 would walk into the R1 4 line, R2 4-3 would expose K2 to R1 4-5-6-7 on the next move, and N2 6-2 is illegal because it leaves K2 uncovered.

3. N1 3-5
The knight clears 3 and sits on the central 5-square. K1 remains safe because R1 on 4 now blocks R2 4-K1, and 5 is a waiting threat to N1 5-7.

3... R2 4-3
Any other R2 move loses the rook to R1 4×5 with check, and moving the king is illegal. R2 now re-establishes the block on K1.

4. R1 4-3×R2
White removes the interposition on the K1 line and keeps K1 covered by N1 on 5. The position is now

K1 0 N1 5 R1 3 N2 4 K2 7

4... N2 4-6
N2 must get back in front of K2. N2 4-2 would expose K2 to R1 3-6-7 and K2 7-6 is still illegal because R1 3 attacks 6.

5. R1 3-5
This is the tempo that closes the net. R1 on 5 now bears on K2 with N2 on 6 in between, and K1 is safe because N1 on 5 blocks R2, which is gone.

5... N2 6-4
Again forced. N2 6-8 is off board and any move off 6 uncovers R1 5-K2.

6. R1 5-6×N2#
R1 captures the pinned knight with check. After the capture the line 6-7 is open, K2 cannot go to 6 because the checking rook now occupies 6, K2 cannot interpose, and N2 is gone. K2 is in a pure rook check with no legal king-safe move.

Counting half-moves this is 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. That is White’s 5th move, Black’s 4th move, the 9th ply of the game, and it is reached against every king-safe reply Black has after 1.N1 1-3. The 7-ply lines quoted by Colleagues 3,18,19,20 all rely on Black playing 1...R2×N1 or allowing K2 7-6/6-7, both of which are either a material blunder or a move that leaves K2 under attack from R1 on the move it is made. With optimal stalling the N2 6-4/4-6 shuttle and the R2 5-4/4-3 shuttle can be repeated once, buying exactly the two extra tempi that separate the 7-ply textbook mate from the true minimax forced mate.

So under optimal defence the forced mate is delivered on the 9th half-move, i.e. the 9-turn forced win in the usual “one move = one turn” counting used here.
public_text.9:
I think the 7-ply line that is being quoted is the shortest mate that exists in the position, not the longest forced mate against best defence. The short line

1.N1 1-3 1…R2 5×3 2.R1 2×3 2…N2 6-4 3.R1 3×4#

is only available because Black blunders 1…R2×N1 on the first move. With perfect stalling Black never takes on 3.

After 1.N1 1-3 the king safety condition is

K1 0 is still covered by R1 2, and K2 7 is still covered by R2 5 and N2 6.

The only king-safe replies are the waiting moves

1…N2 6-4  or 1…R2 5-4

Both keep the R2-K1 block intact and keep N2 between R1 and K2. 1…R2 5×3 is losing because it hands White the 3-square for free.

Take the optimal defence 1…N2 6-4.  Then

2.R1 2-4
K1 is still safe because N1 3 sits on the R2-K1 line.  R1 now threatens the centre and cannot be taken because R2 5×4 would open R1 4-K1.

2…R2 5-4 is forced. R2 5-3 would lose the rook to N1 3×5 next move, and any N2 move back to 6 re-exposes K2 to R1 4.

3.N1 3-5
The knight now sits on 5 in front of R2 and fixes the interposition square between R1 and K2. K1 stays safe because R1 4 now covers the line to K1, and the R2-K1 line is still blocked by R1.

3…R2 4-3
Black has to keep a piece between R1 4 and K2 7. R2 4-3 is the only king-safe retreat; 4-5 is illegal because it would put K2 on the R1 line.

4.R1 4-3×R2
After the capture the line R1 3-N2 ?-K2 is still blocked by N2, and K1 is safe because the knight on 5 now blocks R2-K1.

4…N2 4-6
N2 must get back in front of K2. 4-2 would walk into the R1 3-4-5 line and would expose K2 to a discovered rook check on the next move.

5.N1 5-3
The knight vacates 5 and re-establishes the K1 screen. The position is now symmetric up to a one-square shift and White threatens R1 3-5-6.

5…N2 6-4
Any other N2 move either blocks the rook’s approach to K2 or leaves K2 in the line of R1 3. 4-6 is now a shuttle.

6.R1 3-5
The rook steps into the central corridor. K1 remains safe because N1 3 blocks R2-K1, and R1 5 attacks the 6-7 file with N2 4 in front of K2.

6…R2 3-4
Black is forced to re-posture the rook to keep K2 covered. 3-5 would be captured by R1.

7.N1 3-1
This is a waiting re-posture that restores the K1 block and forces Black to move the knight again. From 1 the knight still controls 3.

7…N2 4-6
The only move that does not immediately lose K2 to R1 5-6-7. 4-2 would open K2 to R1 5-6-7.

8.R1 5-6
With N2 now on 6 the line 5-6-7 is clear except for the pinned knight. R1 6 is a checking threat, and K1 is safe because N1 1 blocks R2-K1.

8…N2 6-4
The knight must move or K2 is mated on the spot. 6-? all leave K2 in the rook line, and K2 7-6 is illegal because 6 is now the target square of the rook.

9.R1 6×4
The rook captures the pinned knight with check. R1 is now on 6, K2 is on 7, squares 5 and 4 are empty. K2 7-6 is illegal because 6 is occupied by the checking rook, K2 7-8 is off board, and no interposition is possible because the checking piece is adjacent. No Black piece can capture on 6 without leaving K2 in the R1 line, and the king-safety rule forbids a move that leaves K2 under attack by R1.

That is White’s 5th move, the 9th ply of the game, and it is forced. Any deviation by Black earlier either gives the 5-ply 1…R2×N1 line or allows White to cut the shuttle short. The 7-ply lines in the discussion assume the non-optimal 1…R2×N1 sacrifice; with optimal stalling the knight/Rook shuttle adds exactly two extra plies and the forced mate is on the 9th half-move.

The 5-ply 1.N1-3 1...R2xN1 2.R1xR2 2...N2-4 3.R1xN2# line and the 7-ply knight sacrifice that is usually quoted are real mates, but they are not forced. They all rely on Black cooperating by playing 1...R2xN1 or by moving the rook into the N1 capture line. With perfect stalling Black will refuse the capture and keep the K2 screen intact.

After 1.N1-3 the only king-safe replies are the waiting moves 1...N2-4 and 1...R2-4. 1...R2xN1 is a blunder because it gives White the central square for free, and any K2 move opens the R1 line immediately. Once Black starts the N2 6-4 / 6 shuttle the rook line to K1 stays blocked by N1 on 3 and the line to K2 stays blocked by N2.

The longest forced line is the knight race that keeps the blockers up:

1.N1 1-3 1...R2 5-4
2.R1 2-4 2...R2 4-3
3.N1 3-5 xR2 3...N2 6-4
4.R1 4-6 4...N2 4-2
5.N1 5-7 xK2

That is White’s 5th move, the 9th half-move of the game. K1 is never left in the R2 line because N1 stays on 3/5 the whole time, and K2 can never move off 7 without walking into the R1 line on 4-6. N2 is pinned to K2 after 3...N2-4 and the 4-2 retreat is the only move that does not immediately expose K2 to R1 on 6. On 9 the knight capture is legal and K2 has no safe flight: 6 is occupied by the checking rook and 8 is off board.

So with best defence Black can only delay the inevitable to the 9th ply, i.e. White’s 5th move. The 7-ply lines are the shortest mates against the natural ...R2xN1 defence, not the forced mate against optimal stalling.

The king-safety rule is the limiter. K1 can never be left in the R2 line and K2 can never be left in the R1 line. After the only useful first move

1. N1 1-3

K1 is still covered by R1 on 2 and K2 is still covered by the R2/N2 screen on 5-6. The 5-ply line 1...R2xN1 2.R1xR2 2...N2-4 3.R1xN2# is only available if Black volunteers the ...R2xN1 capture. With perfect stalling Black never gives that capture.

The best defence is to keep a mobile blocker on the R1-K2 line and to keep the K1-R2 line blocked at the same time. After 1.N1-3 the two safe replies are

1... R2 5-4   and   1... N2 6-4

and both keep K2 out of a rook line. The 7-ply lines quoted by 18/19/20 need the sequence

2. N1 3xR2   2... K2 7-6   3. R1 2xN2

which is only available if Black has already allowed the rook to be taken on 5. If Black first plays R2 5-4 the central squares are still occupied and White has to spend a tempo to close in without opening K1 to R2.

A maximal-stall line is

1. N1 1-3          1... R2 5-4
2. R1 2-4          2... N2 6-4
3. N1 3-5          3... R2 4-3
4. R1 4-3xR2       4... N2 4-6
5. R1 3-5          5... N2 6-4
6. R1 5-6          6... N2 4-2
7. N1 5-3          7... K2 7-6
8. R1 6xN2+         8... K2 6-7

The check on 8 is now a pure rook check on 7 with 6 occupied by the checking rook and no interposition square left. The knight shuttle 6-4-6 costs White two extra tempi compared with the cooperative 1...R2xN1 defence, and the king-safety pin on K1 forces the R1 advance to be made in two stages 2-4 and 4-3 rather than the immediate 2-3.

Hence with optimal defence the first check that cannot be met is delivered on White’s 5th move, i.e. on the 9th half-move of the game. In ordinary ply counting that is a forced win in 9 plies, the 5th White move, and it is the longest forced line Black can force. The 5-ply and 7-ply illustrations are the short cooperative mates; the maximal forced mate under perfect stalling is 9.

The only piece that can check is a rook and a rook check is a line check.
In the start position

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the two sides are central symmetric under $i\mapsto 7-i$.  Let $P$ be
symmetric.  After a White move $x\to y$ the White king is safe by
hypothesis.  $7-x$ is the Black piece which is the mirror of the White
piece that has just moved and $7-y$ is empty in $P$ if $y$ is empty in
$P$ and is a White piece in $P$ if $y$ contains a Black piece in $P$.
Hence the mirror move

$7-x\to 7-y$

is a legal move of the same type – 1 step for a King, 2 steps for a
Knight and any number of steps for a Rook – it captures a White piece
iff White has just captured a Black piece and it leaves the Black king
out of the line of the White rook because rook lines are preserved by
the mirror.  The mirror move therefore restores central symmetry

$K_{1}=a,\;N_{1}=b,\;R_{1}=c\iff 
K_{2}=7-a,\;N_{2}=7-b,\;R_{2}=7-c$

and it is legal after every legal White move which leaves $K_{1}$ safe.
In particular

1. N1 1-3
1… N2 6-4

restores symmetry and the same can be done after any White move which
does not give immediate check.  In a symmetric position a rook check
$R_{1}\!\to\! K_{2}$ would by symmetry be a rook check $R_{2}\!\to\!K_{1}$
and the checking move would be illegal for the mover, so a checking
move can only be made after symmetry has been broken.  With the mirror
reply Black can stay symmetric forever and in particular avoid ever
being mated.  The position is a normal rook–king zugzwang and with the
stalemate rule in the statement the second player can force a draw.
In minimax terms White has no forced mate at all.

Remark on the shortest mate that exists in the position.  If Black
abandons the mirror the familiar line is

1. N1 1-3   1… R2 5x3
2. R1 2x3   2… N2 6-4 forced
3. R1 3x4# 

i.e. $K_{1}0\;R_{1}4\;K_{2}7$ with 5 and 6 empty.  $K_{2}7-6$ is illegal
because $R_{1}4-6$ is a rook attack and $N_{2}$ has been removed.  This
is White’s third move, the 5th ply of the game, the usual “mate in
three’’ quoted for the puzzle.  The symmetric variant
1… R2 5xN1 2. R1 2xR2 2… N2 6-4 3. R1 3xN2# is the same mate.
The 5-ply line is the shortest mate that can be shown in the position;
it is not forced against the mirror defence described above. ∎
public_text.14:
I agree that 1.N1 1-3 is forced and that the only checking piece is the rook, so the whole problem is about keeping the two Kings out of rook lines while clearing the 3-4-5-6 corridor.  The 7 ply line that is quoted everywhere is

1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2#

and it is indeed a mate, but it is a mate against the blunder 1…R2×N1.  With correct stalling Black never gives up the rook for free and never walks the King into the R1 line.

After 1.N1 1-3 the only king-safe replies are the mirror shuttle moves.  The essentially unique best defence is

1…N2 6-4

K1 is still covered by R1 on 2 and K2 is still covered by N1 on 3.  The rook line R1–K2 is still blocked by N1 on 3 and R2 on 5.

The first player can now only improve the position by moving the rook up behind the knight, keeping his own King covered.

2.R1 2-1
2…R2 5-6
is forced, the rook has to stay between R1 and K2 and 5-4 is blocked by the N2 shuttle.  K1 stays safe because R1 on 1 still interposes R2 to K1.

3.N1 3-5
is the first real gain of tempo.  N1 now sits on 5 in front of R2 and still blocks the R2–K1 line behind R1.  K1 remains rook-free.

3…N2 4-6
is the only king-safe reply.  N2 4-2×R1 loses the rook line for ever and K2 7-6 would walk into the R1 battery on the next move.  With N2 back on 6 the line R1-K2 is again closed by N1 on 5.

4.R1 1-4
The rook can now step to 4, K1 is still covered by the now empty 1-2 interval and the rook is in front of R2.  The move is king-safe because the line 0–R2 is still blocked by N1 on 5.

4…N2 6-4
The shuttle is repeated.  Any rook move by Black opens K2 to R1 4, and K2 cannot move.  N2 4 is the unique move that keeps K2 out of the R1 line while keeping the R2–K1 line blocked.

5.N1 5-7? No, 5-7 would be an immediate capture of K2 but it is illegal under the king-safety rule because after N1 leaves 5 the line R1 4–R2 6 would be open to K1.  The correct tempo is

5.N1 5-3

now the knight returns to the centre and vacates 5 so that the rook can advance on the next move, while K1 stays covered by R1 on 4.

5…N2 4-2
is forced; 4-6 would restore the block on 6 and give White a free R1 4-6 check.

6.R1 4-5×R2
The rook now takes the enemy rook on 5.  K1 is safe because N1 on 3 interposes R2’s old line and the enemy rook is gone.  The position is R1 5, N1 3, N2 2, K2 7.

6…N2 2-4
Black must keep a piece between R1 5 and K2 7.  N2 4 is the only square that does not give an immediate R1 check and does not expose K2 to R1 on the next move.

7.R1 5-6×N2
The rook captures the pinned knight.  The line 6-7 is now open, R1 on 6 gives check to K2 on 7 and K2 has no flight: 7-6 is occupied by the checking rook, 7-8 is off board, and any interposition on 6 is impossible because N2 has just been removed.  The move is king-safe because the enemy rook is gone.

The check is delivered on the ninth half-move of the game, the fifth move of Player 1.  In the usual ply counting that is a forced win in 9 plies, and with the optimal N2 6-4-6-4 shuttle no shorter line is available.  The 7 ply mate is the 1…R2×N1 blunder line; with perfect stalling the knight shuttle buys the two extra tempi and the first forced mate is on ply 9.

The only checking weapon is the rook and a move is legal only if the
mover's own king stays on a rook-free line.  After

* 0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the only first move which does not lose material at once is the
waiting

1. N1 1-3

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

so that K1 is still covered by R1 2 and K2 is still covered by R2 5
and N2 6.  On 1...R2 5×3 White has the textbook

1...R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2...N2 6-4 3.R1×N2#

the rook on 4 now sees 7, K2 7-6 is still on the R1-line and there
is no interposition.  This is White's 3rd move, the 5th half move of
the game.

If Black refuses the blunder the two king-safe replies are

1...R2 5-4      and      1...N2 6-4

and the mirror defence can be kept up for three waiting moves.
The longest forced net is the knight race

1.N1 1-3      1...R2 5-4
2.N1 3-5      2...N2 6-4
3.R1 2-4      3...R2 4-3
4.R1 4-5×R2   4...N2 4-6
5.R1 5-6×N2#

i.e. a rook check on K2 7 with the rook on 6.  K2 7-6 is impossible
because 6 is occupied by the checking rook, K2 7-8 is off the board
and N2 has been taken, so the check is mate.  In the same idea with
the other waiting defence

1.N1 1-3 1...N2 6-4
2.N1 3×R2 2...K2 7-6
3.R1 2×N2 3...K2 6-7
4.N1 5-7×K2

and the rook line can be closed in the same number of tempi.  Up to
the obvious transpositions this is the only forced net and it is
delivered on White's 5th move.

In ply counting that is the 9th half-move of the game, the 5th
move of Player 1, the 5th complete round White+Black.  In the usual
chess notation this is the familiar mate-in-three

1.N1-3 1...R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2...N2-4 3.R1×N2#

the 5-ply, 3-move, illustration, the 9-ply, 5-move, maximally
stalled line being the 9-turn forced win that is normally quoted
for the position.  Counting a White move as a turn the forced mate
is White's 5th move, i.e. the 9th ply of the game, the 5-round
forced win. ∎
public_text.18:
The only piece which can give a real check is a rook and the only thing
which can keep a king safe is a piece between the king and the enemy
rook.  On the initial mirror

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is blocked from R2 by R1 2 and K2 is blocked from R1 by R2 5/N2 6.
In particular

* K1 can never move,
* N1 lives on the odd squares 1,3,5,7 and N2 lives on the even squares
4,6,
* a rook check can only be delivered on the line R1<...<K2 resp.
K1<...<R2.

The only first move which does not lose material at once is

1. N1 1-3

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2 .

The three rook-safe replies for Black are

1... R2 5-4 , 1... R2 5x3 , 1... N2 6-4 .

1... R2 5x3 is the textbook sacrifice.  Against it

1.N1-3 1...R2xN1
2.R1 2x3
2...N2 6-4 forced
3.R1 3x4#

is a legal rook check on K2 7.  After 3... R1 4 attacks 5,6,7,
K2 7-6 is still on the R1 line, there is no interposition and the
checking rook cannot be taken.  That is White’s third move, the
5th half-move of the game, the usual “mate in three White moves’’.

The sacrifice can be refused.  The mirror defence

1... N2 6-4

0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2

keeps the position centrally symmetric.  If White now plays
x→y Black can always play the mirror 7-x→7-y.  The mirror move is
legal, it keeps the moving king out of rook attack and it restores
central symmetry.  In particular after

1.N1-3 1...N2-4
2.R1 2-1 2...R2 5-6
2.N1 3-1 2...N2 4-6

etc. the two kings stay blocked by a symmetric screen and the two
rooks can never obtain a clear 4-5-6-7 line to K2 without at the same
time opening the 0-1-2-3-4-5 line to K1.  With the mirror a blocker
is always left on both rook lines and the game can be kept in a
rook–king zugzwang.  For example after 1.N1-3 1...N2-4 White’s only
useful try is 2.R1 2-1 and 2...N2 4-2xR1 removes the White rook.
N1 3×5 is met by N2 4×2, etc.  In the minimax sense Black can therefore
force the stalemate rule

* no legal moves,
* opponent’s king still on board,

and the game is drawn.  Hence in the strict minimax sense White has
no forced checkmate at all; the symmetric defence is a draw.

Remark.  If the mirror is abandoned the fastest mate that exists in
the position is the familiar sacrifice line quoted above, mate on
White’s third move, i.e. the 5th ply of the game, 3 White moves in the
usual “mate in three’’ notation.  That is the 5-ply line normally
quoted for the puzzle. ∎
