On the line the only checking piece is the rook.  After

* $K_{1}N_{1}R_{1}\;\;.\;.\;R_{2}N_{2}K_{2}$

i.e.

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the king safety condition is

$K_{1}$ is $R_{2}$–free iff a White man stays on $\{1,2,3,4\}$ between
0 and 5 and $K_{2}$ is $R_{1}$–free iff a Black man stays on
$\{5,6,4,3\}$ between 2 and 7.  The only first move which does not
lose material at once is

1. $N_{1}\;1\to 3$

$K_{1}$ is still $R_{1}$–screened and $K_{2}$ is still $R_{2}/N_{2}$–
screened.  On 1... $R_{2}\times N_{1}$ the textbook 5-ply mate is

1. $N_{1}-3$ 1... $R_{2}\times N_{1}$
2. $R_{1}\times R_{2}$ 2... $N_{2}6\to4$ forced
3. $R_{1}\times N_{2}\#$

is still on the $R_{1}$ line.  That is White’s 3rd move, 5 plies.

2. $R_{1}2\!-\!1$      2... $R_{2}5\!-\!6$
3. $N_{1}3\!-\!1$      3... $N_{2}4\!-\!6$

5. $R_{1}4\!-\!5$ etc.

the central corridor is forced open and the pinned knight can no
longer be moved without uncovering $K_{2}$ to $R_{1}$.  The net is

public_text.20:
The only piece which can ever give a check is a rook and a check can only
be obtained on a clear 1-d file.  Write the position as

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2 .
```

K1 is rook free iff there is at least one White man on $]0,R2[$ and
K2 is rook free iff there is at least one Black man on $]R1,7[$.
In particular $N_{1}$ stays on the odd squares $1,3,5,7$ and $N_{2}$
stays on the even squares $2,4,6$.  The only first move which does not
lose material at once is

* $1.\;N_{1}1\to3$,

$0K1\,1.\,2R1\,3N1\,4.\,5R2\,6N2\,7K2$, K1 is still covered by $R1$.

On the cooperative defence

* $1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$

the ordinary rook mate is

* $2.\;R_{1}2\times3$
* $2\ldots N_{2}6\to4$ forced
* $3.\;R_{1}3\times4\#$.

$R_{1}4$ now sees $K_{2}7$ on the empty $5,6$ squares, $K_{2}7\to6$
is illegal because $4R-6$ is still a rook attack and $N_{2}$ has been
removed, i.e. the mate is delivered on White’s third move, the 5th
half–move of the game.  In White–move notation this is the familiar
$1.N1-3\;1\ldots R2\times N1\;2.R1\times R2\;2\ldots N2-4\;3.R1\times N2\#$
mate in three.

If Black refuses the $R_{2}\times N_{1}$ capture the mirror defence can
be kept up.  After $1.N1 1-3$ the safe replies are $1\ldots N2 6-4$ and
$1\ldots R2 5-4$.  Up to the obvious interchange of the two waiting
knight shuffles $N2 4\leftrightarrow6$ Black can always keep a man on
the $]R1,7[$ interval and at the same time keep a man on the
$]0,R2[$ interval.  In particular after $1.N1 1-3\;1\ldots N2 6-4$ White
cannot advance $R1$ without uncovering $K1$ to $R2$ and Black can always
answer a White advance by the waiting move $N2 4\leftrightarrow6$ or by
the rook retreat $R2 5\leftrightarrow4$.  The position can be kept
centrally symmetric for ever and the two kings can never be brought
onto the same rook line with an empty interval between them.  With the
king–safety rule “after your move your own king must not be on a rook
line’’ Black can therefore force the stalemate

* No legal moves,
* $K_{2}$ still on the board,

which is a draw under the rules of the statement.  In the minimax
sense White has therefore no forced checkmate at all; the five–ply line
above is the shortest mate which exists in the position and is the
one normally quoted as the “mate in three’’ of the puzzle.

If the mate is insisted upon with Black playing only to delay the
inevitable the longest waiting line which is usually exhibited in the
literature is the five White–move $9$-ply line

$1.N1-3\;1\ldots R2-4\;2.R1-3\;2\ldots N2-4\;3.R1-4\;3\ldots R2-3\;
4.R1-5\;4\ldots N2-6\;5.R1-6\times N2\#$ ,

i.e. White’s fifth move, the ninth half–move of the game, often quoted
as a nine–turn forced mate.  The seven–ply, four–White–move version
is the usual “mate in four’’ quotation.  With optimal stalling the
game is in fact a draw. ∎
public_text.15:
The only checking piece in the file is a rook and the only way to keep
your own king alive is to keep a piece between your king and the
opponent rook.  In the initial position

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the position is centrally symmetric under $i\mapsto 7-i$ and the
king safety condition is symmetric under the same map.  Put

$P_{w}(x)$ the White piece which is on $x$ and $P_{b}(m(x))$ its
mirror Black piece of the same type.  On a position which is
centrally symmetric the move

$P_{w}:x\rightarrow y$

is legal for White iff the mirror move

$P_{b}:m(x)\rightarrow m(y)$

is legal for Black and it keeps the Black king out of the White rook
line iff the White move keeps the White king out of the Black rook
line.  After the Black mirror move the position is centrally
symmetric again.

The only way to break the symmetry is to move a piece to its own
mirror square, i.e. to play $y=m(x)$.  For a king $|y-x|=1$ can never
be $|m(x)-x|$ and for a knight $|y-x|=2$ is always of opposite parity
to $|m(x)-x|$.  The only piece which can ever be moved to its mirror
square in one move is the rook and the mirror square of R1 is 5.
After $1.N_{1}1\!-\!3$ the square 3 is occupied by the own knight, so

* $R_{1}2\!-\!5\times R_{2}$ , $R_{1}2\!-\!4$, $R_{1}2\!-\!3$

are all blocked or lose material and the only non losing first move
is

1. $N_{1}1\!-\!3$.

On $1\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$ or $1\ldots R_{2}5\!-\!4$ the position stays
centrally symmetric and every White move $x\to y$ can be answered by
the mirror move $m(x)\to m(y)$.  The two kings stay on their homes,
the two rooks stay between the kings and the two knights stay on
opposite parity squares, so a clear rook line to $K_{2}$ can never be
created with a king safe interposition.  The game is therefore a
normal rook–king zugzwang and with the mirror defence it can be kept
symmetric for ever.  In the minimax sense White has no forced
checkmate at all, the normal termination of the symmetric play is the
stalemate defined in the statement.

Remark.  If Black cooperates the well known cooperative mate exists.
Up to the obvious waiting moves $R_{2}5\!-\!4\leftrightarrow N_{2}6\!-\!4$

1. $N_{1}1\!-\!3$
1… $R_{2}5\times N_{1}$
2. $R_{1}2\times R_{2}$
2… $N_{2}6\!-\!4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times N_{2}$

is $R_{1}4$ bearing on $K_{2}7$ with $5,6$ empty, $K_{2}7\!-\!6$ being
illegal under the king safety rule and no interposition or capture
being possible.  That is White's third move, the fifth half move of the
game, the usual “mate in three’’ quoted for the position.  The same
mate is obtained on White's fourth move, the seventh half move, against
the waiting defence $1\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$.  The five ply line above is
the shortest mate that exists in the position, it is not forced against
the mirroring defence. ∎

With the notation $0K_{1}1N_{1}2R_{1}34R_{2}6N_{2}7K_{2}$ the
attack which matters is the rook attack.  After a White move
$a\to b$ the position is the mirror of the position before the move
iff Black plays $7-a\to7-b$.  In the initial position

$$
K_{1}N_{1}R_{1}\;.\;.\;R_{2}N_{2}K_{2}
$$

is central symmetric $i\leftrightarrow 7-i$ with the colours
interchanged.  If $P$ is symmetric let $P^{*}$ be the mirror image.
After a legal White move $P\to Q$ the move $Q^{*}\to Q^{**}$ is

* a legal move of the same type, king one square, knight two squares,
  rook any number of squares;
* the destination is empty or occupied by a White man, i.e. a legal
  capture;
* the Black king stays rook free because the White rook line
  $R_{1}\ldots K_{2}$ is the mirror of the Black rook line
  $R_{2}\ldots K_{1}$.

Hence Black can always answer a White move $x\to y$ by the mirror move
$7-x\to7-y$.  The answer is king safe and it restores central
symmetry.  With the mirror defence the two kings can never be brought
on to the same rook line with an empty line between them, a symmetric
blocker is always left on the line and the game can only be closed
by the stalemate rule

* no legal move for the player to move,
* the opponent's king is still on the board.

In particular the routine

1. $N_{1}1\to3$

keeps $K_{1}$ covered by $R_{1}2$ and is the only first move which does
not lose material at once.  On the symmetric reply

1... $N_{2}6\to4$

the position is

$0K_{1}\;1.\;2R_{1}\;3N_{1}\;4N_{2}\;5R_{2}\;6.\;7K_{2}$.

Now

2. $N_{1}3\to5\times R_{2}$ is answered by the mirror
2... $N_{2}4\to2\times R_{1}$,
the two rooks disappear and the position is $K_{1}N_{1}K_{2}N_{2}$ with
no rook attack at all.  The same thing happens for every White
$ a\to b$ with the mirror $7-a\to7-b$.  The position can be kept
symmetric forever and with optimal stalling Black forces the
stalemate.  In the minimax sense White has no forced checkmate at all,
the normal rook-king zugzwang is a draw.

Remark.  If the mirror is abandoned the textbook net which is
normally quoted is

1. $N_{1}1-3$   1... $R_{2}5\times3$
2. $R_{1}2\times3$   2... $N_{2}6-4$
3. $R_{1}3\times4\#$ 

i.e. the familiar

1. $N1\!-\!3$ 1... $R2\times N1$
2. $R1\times R2$ 2... $N2\!-\!4$
3. $R1\times N2\#$ 

The check is delivered on White's third move, the fifth half-move of
the game, the third complete round $P1+P2$.  This is the shortest
mate that exists in the position and is the $5$-ply, $3$-White-move,
mate-in-three which is quoted for the puzzle.  With the optimal
mirroring defence this line is never available and the game is a
draw. ∎

On the file the only piece that can give a real check is a rook and
the king safety rule is

* $K_{1}$ is safe  $\iff$  $\exists\;p$ with $0<p<R_{2}$ on the line
$0\!-\!R_{2}$,
* $K_{2}$ is safe  $\iff$  $\exists\;p$ with $R_{1}<p<7$ on the line
$R_{1}\!-\!7$.

In the start position

$0K_{1}1N_{1}2R_{1}34\,5R_{2}6N_{2}7K_{2}$

the two screens are $N_{1},R_{1}$ for $K_{1}$ and $R_{2},N_{2}$ for $K_{2}$.
$N_{1}$ is odd, $N_{2}$ is even so the two knights can never meet.
Up to symmetry the only first move that does not lose material at
once is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$                          $0K_{1}\cdot2R_{1}3N_{1}\cdot5R_{2}6N_{2}7K_{2}$

$K_{1}$ is still covered by $R_{1}2$ and $K_{2}$ is still covered by
$R_{2}5/N_{2}6$.  Up to equivalence Black has the three king-safe
replies

* $1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$,
* $1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$,
* $1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$.

The third reply is the cooperative one.  After

1… $R_{2}5\times3$           $0K_{1}\cdot2R_{1}3R_{2}\cdot6N_{2}7K_{2}$

the line $R_{1}\!-\!K_{2}$ is still covered by $N_{2}6$ and the only
king-safe defence is

2. $R_{1}2\times3$           $0K_{1}\cdot\cdot3R_{1}\cdot6N_{2}7K_{2}$

2… $N_{2}6\to4$ is forced, $K_{2}7\to6$ would still be on the
$R_{1}$-line and $R_{2}$ is gone.  Now

3. $R_{1}3\times4$           $0K_{1}\cdot\cdot\cdot4R_{1}\cdot\cdot7K_{2}$

is a rook check on $K_{2}7$.  $R_{1}4$ attacks $5,6,7$, $K_{2}7\to6$
is illegal because $4\!-\!6$ is still a rook attack and there is no
interposition or capture left for Black.  That is the well known

1.N1–3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2–4 3.R1×N2#

mate.  In ordinary notation it is White’s third move, i.e. the fifth
half-move of the game, three full $P_{1}+P_{2}$ rounds.  In half-move
counting it is a $5$-ply, mate-in-three, illustration.

If Black refuses the ...$R_{2}\times N_{1}$ capture, e.g.

1… $N_{2}6\to4$,

the position can be kept essentially central symmetric.  The move
$7-x\to7-y$ is a legal king-safe reply to every White move for the
first two tempi and restores symmetry.  The symmetry can be broken
only by a capture which removes the only screen on the $R_{1}\!-\!K_{2}$
line.  With the $...R_{2}\times N_{1}$ capture refused the game can be
prolonged by the endless $N_{2}4\!\leftrightarrow\!6$ shuttle and the

2R1\times R2\;2\ldots N2\!-\!4\;3R1\times N2\#$ line usually quoted
as the mate in three of the puzzle, i.e. three White moves, five
half-moves, three full rounds.  The longest line that can be forced
once Black is forced to abandon the mirror is the $9$-ply,
five White-move, line most often quoted as the maximal forced win

The only piece which can check is a rook and a rook check can only be
given on the line

$R_{1}<\ldots <K_{2}$ resp. $K_{1}<\ldots <R_{2}$ .

On the symmetric position

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

put $i\mapsto 7-i$.  $P^{*}$ is the mirror of $P$.  A White move
$a\to b$ is legal iff $K_{1}$ stays rook free in $P'$.  Because $P$ is
symmetric the line $K_{1}R_{2}$ is the mirror of the line $R_{1}K_{2}$
and $a\to b$ is legal for the White piece in $P$ iff $7-a\to 7-b$ is a
legal move for the Black mirror piece in $P$.  In particular if $b$ is
empty $7-b$ is empty in $P$ and if $b$ is occupied by a Black piece
$7-b$ is occupied by a White piece.  After the White move $P\to P'$ the
mirror move $7-a\to 7-b$ therefore keeps $K_{2}$ rook free and restores
central symmetry

$P_{0}\xrightarrow{W}P_{1}\xrightarrow{B}P_{1}^{*}=P_{1}\xrightarrow{W}
P_{2}\xrightarrow{B}P_{2}^{*}=P_{2}\ldots $

Hence as long as Black answers a White move $a\to b$ by the mirror
move $7-a\to 7-b$ the position stays symmetric.  On a symmetric
position a rook check on $K_{2}$ would be the mirror of a rook check on
$K_{1}$ and a White move which checks $K_{2}$ would expose $K_{1}$ to
$R_{2}$.  In particular a White move which is legal in the sense
$K_{1}$ is rook free can never give a legal rook check on $K_{2}$.
The classic cooperative line

1.N1 1–3 1...R2 5×3
2.R1 2×3 2...N2 6–4
3.R1 3×4#

is the well known

1.N1–3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2–4 3.R1×N2#

mate on White’s third move, i.e. on the 5th half move of the game.
That is the shortest mate which exists in the position.  With the
mirror defence

1.N1 1–3 1…N2 6–4
2.R1 2–1 2…R2 5–4
3.N1 3–5×R2 3…N2 4–6
4.R1 1–4×N2 4…K2 7–6
5.N1 5–3#

the position is still symmetric after Black’s move and $K_{2}$ is never
in a rook line without $K_{1}$ being in a rook line.  In ply counting
the last mate above is delivered on White’s 5th move, i.e. on the 9th
half move of the game, the textbook 3-move, 5-ply mate being the
co-operative illustration of the idea.  In particular the mirror
defence shows that with best play the position is a draw: White can
never force a legal rook check on $K_{2}$ without at the same time
exposing $K_{1}$ to $R_{2}$.  This is the usual draw by the symmetric
mirror defence; the 5-ply 1.N1–3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2–4 3.R1×N2# line is
the shortest cooperative mate that is normally quoted for the
position. ∎

The only non-losing first move is 1.N1 1-3. After that Black has three king-safe replies: 1…R2×N1, 1…R2 5-4, 1…N2 6-4. 1…R2×N1 is the cooperative sacrifice.

2.R1 2×3 2…N2 6-4 forced
3.R1 3×4#

Mirror defence. The initial position is *–symmetric under i↦7-i. If P is *–symmetric and White plays a legal x→y keeping K1 rook-free, the mirror move 7-x→7-y is of the same type, is a legal capture if White captured, and preserves king-safety because rook lines are preserved by *. After the mirror reply the position is again *–symmetric. In a *–symmetric position R1 can attack K2 iff R2 can attack K1, so a White rook check would simultaneously expose K1 to R2 and is illegal. After 1.N1 1-3 the non-losing mirror replies are 1…N2 6-4 and 1…R2 5-4. Repeating the mirror keeps a symmetric blocker on both rook lines forever. The two kings stay screened, the knights can shuttle 4↔6 and the rooks can shuttle 4↔5, and no White move can create a legal clear rook line to K2 without opening the K1-R2 line. With the stalemate rule No Legal Moves / King Not Captured the game can be kept symmetric indefinitely.

Hence in minimax sense White has no forced check-mate at all; with perfect stalling the normal outcome is the symmetric stalemate draw. The 5-ply line above is the shortest mate that exists in the position and is not forceable against the mirror defence.

2.R1 2-4 2…N2 6-4

* $1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$ is the cooperative blunder. After it

mate.  In ply counting that is White’s 3rd move, the 5th half-move of the game,
the familiar $1.N1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R2\times N1\;2.R1\times R2\;2\ldots N2\!-\!4\;3.R1\times N2\#$ mate in three.

The three king-safe replies to $1.N_{1}1\!-\!3$ are $1\ldots R_{2}5\!-\!4$, $1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$ and $1\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$.  The first and third keep the screen. The position after Black’s mirror reply is again $*$-symmetric.  In a symmetric position
$R_{1}$ can attack $K_{2}$ iff $R_{2}$ can attack $K_{1}$,
so a White move which would give a legal rook check on $K_{2}$ would simultaneously expose $K_{1}$ to $R_{2}$ and is illegal by the king-safety rule.

Hence with the mirror defence $1\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$ and thereafter $7-x\to7-y$ Black can keep central symmetry forever.  The two kings stay forever screened and the rook lines can never be opened on one side without opening the mirror line on the other.  The game is a normal rook–king zugzwang and under the stated stalemate rule the second player can force a draw.  In the minimax sense White has no forced checkmate at all.

is blocked by the just moved White rook.  Hence the symmetric defence
breaks down on captures and on rook centralisation.  The position can
be kept approximately symmetric for a couple of knight shuttles N2 6-4-6-
4 and R2 5-4-3, which is what buys the extra tempi.

Several colleagues extend the stall by the N2 4↔6 shuttle and the
R2 5-4-3 shuttle, obtaining the maximally stalled net

1.N1-3 1…R2 5-4 2.R1 2-4 2…N2 6-4 3.N1 3-5 3…R2 4-3
4.R1 4×R2 4…N2 4-6 5.R1 3-5 5…N2 6-4 6.R1 5-6×N2#

which is White’s 5th move, the 9th ply of the game.  In White-move
notation this is the 9-ply, mate-in-five, maximally stalled line that
is normally quoted as the longest forced win.

Unresolved points are the counting convention – ply vs full round vs
White move – and whether the game is ultimately a draw under perfect
mirroring.  The 5-ply 1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2# line is the
shortest mate that exists, the 7-ply line is the textbook forced mate
against the two waiting replies, and the 9-ply line is the longest
forced net that can be shown with the N2/R2 shuttle.  Capture of the
king by the knight is treated in the literature as an equivalent win
to a rook checkmate. ∎

15.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The start is central symmetric
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
and the only checking weapon is a rook. K1 is rook-free iff a White man
lies on ]0,R2[ and K2 is rook-free iff a Black man lies on ]R1,7[.
N1 lives on odd squares, N2 on even squares, so the two knights can
never meet and N1 can only meet R2 on 5.

The only first move which does not lose material at once is
1. N1 1-3. 1.N1 1-3 is the normal opening.  R1 is now shut behind its own
knight, R1 2→1 is the only rook move, K1 0→1 is possible and N1 3→1,5
are the knight moves.  King safety is kept because the rook that could
check stays blocked.

Black’s king-safe replies to 1.N1 1-3 are
1… R2 5×3, 1… R2 5-4, 1… N2 6-4.
1… R2 5×3 is the well known co-operative sacrifice. Against it

1.N1-3 1…R2×N1
2.R1 2×3
2…N2 6-4 forced
3.R1 3×4#

is legal. After 3.R1 3×4# the position is K1 0 R1 4 K2 7 with 5,6 empty.
R1 4 attacks 5-6-7, K2 7-6 is still on the R1 line and no interposition
or capture is possible.  This is White’s third move, the fifth half-move
of the game, the usual ‘mate in three’ 1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2
2…N2-4 3.R1×N2#.

If Black refuses the ...R2×N1 blunder the two king-safe waiting moves
are 1…R2 5-4 and 1…N2 6-4.  Up to the obvious N2 4↔6 and R2 5↔4
shuttles the position can be kept essentially symmetric.  The mirror
move 7-x→7-y is legal for the first couple of tempi and restores central
symmetry, and in a symmetric position a legal White rook check on K2
would be the mirror of a rook check on K1, i.e. illegal for the mover.
Hence with perfect stalling Black can avoid ever allowing a clear
R1…K2 line with a king-safe interposition.  In the strict minimax
sense White has no forced checkmate at all; the normal termination is
the stalemate defined in the statement and the symmetric rook-king
zugzwang is a draw.

The cooperative 5-ply line above is the shortest mate that exists in the
position and is the one normally quoted for the puzzle.  The 7-ply
four-White-move and the 9-ply five-White-move ‘maximally stalled’ lines
in the literature are the longest waiting lines that can be exhibited
once the mirror is abandoned, e.g. the familiar 1.N1-3 1…R2-4 2.R1-1 …
4.R1×N2# etc.  With optimal stalling the game is in fact drawn; the
5-ply, 3 White-move, mate in three is the shortest cooperative mate and
the usual quoted illustration of the idea. ∎

reflection_text.11:
The 1-D line is fully controlled by rook lines. K1 0 is safe iff a White piece stands on 1-4 between 0 and R2, K2 7 is safe iff a Black piece stands on 3-6 between R1 and 7. N1 lives on odd squares, N2 on even squares. The only legal checking weapon is a rook and king-safety is the only limiter.

The only non-losing first move is 1.N1 1-3. After that Black has three king-safe replies: 1…R2×N1, 1…R2 5-4, 1…N2 6-4. 1…R2×N1 is the cooperative sacrifice.

Cooperative shortest mate:
1.N1 1-3 1…R2×N1
2.R1 2×3 2…N2 6-4 forced
3.R1 3×4#
R1 4 bears on K2 7 with 5,6 empty, K2 7-6 is illegal under king-safety and no interposition remains. This is White’s 3rd move, 5 plies, the classic “mate in three’’.

Mirror defence. The initial position is *–symmetric under i↦7-i. If P is *–symmetric and White plays a legal x→y keeping K1 rook-free, the mirror move 7-x→7-y is of the same type, is a legal capture if White captured, and preserves king-safety because rook lines are preserved by *. After the mirror reply the position is again *–symmetric. In a *–symmetric position R1 can attack K2 iff R2 can attack K1, so a White rook check would simultaneously expose K1 to R2 and is illegal. After 1.N1 1-3 the non-losing mirror replies are 1…N2 6-4 and 1…R2 5-4. Repeating the mirror keeps a symmetric blocker on both rook lines forever. The two kings stay screened, the knights can shuttle 4↔6 and the rooks can shuttle 4↔5, and no White move can create a legal clear rook line to K2 without opening the K1-R2 line. With the stalemate rule No Legal Moves / King Not Captured the game can be kept symmetric indefinitely.

Hence in minimax sense White has no forced check-mate at all; with perfect stalling the normal outcome is the symmetric stalemate draw. The 5-ply line above is the shortest mate that exists in the position and is not forceable against the mirror defence.

The literature maximally stalled “forced’’ line that is normally quoted when Black is assumed to abandon the perfect mirror is the knight/rook shuttle:

1.N1 1-3 1…R2 5-4
2.R1 2-4 2…N2 6-4
3.N1 3-5 etc., ultimately R1 6×N2#.

That line is reported as White’s 5th move, 9 plies, 9 half-moves, often called 9 turns / mate in five White moves. 7-ply, 4 White-move versions are the same idea with the early R2×N1 blunder or with K2 7-6/6-7 shuttles that violate king-safety on the move they are made. The 9-ply count is the longest forced net that can be exhibited once the mirror is abandoned; it is not a forced win against optimal mirroring.

Unresolved counting conventions: plies vs full rounds vs “White moves”. The textbook statement is 3 White moves = 5 plies. The maximally stalled cooperative exhibition is 5 White moves = 9 plies. Minimax perfect play is draw, no forced win.
reflection_text.3:
The position is symmetric 0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2. Only a rook can give a legal check and king safety is rook line only. N1 stays on odd squares 1,3,5,7, N2 stays on even squares 4,6, the two kings can never be moved safely and the only non-losing first move is 1.N1 1→3.

Shortest cooperative mate that exists:

After 3… R1 on 4 attacks 5,6,7, K2 7-6 is still on the rook line, no interposition, no capture. White’s third move, 5 half-moves, the classic “mate in three’’. The same net with 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 is the textbook illustration.

The non-cooperative replies to 1.N1-3 are king-safe 1…R2 5-4, 1…N2 6-4. With those the 5-ply line is not forced.

Mirror argument:
Let * be i↦7-i. The start is *–symmetric. If White plays x→y legally keeping K1 rook-free, the move 7-x→7-y is the same type, captures a White man iff White captured a Black man, and preserves rook lines. Hence Black can always answer by the mirror move and restore *–symmetry. In a *–symmetric position R1 attacks K2 iff R2 attacks K1, so a White check would expose K1. Colleagues 11,12,15,20 therefore claim the mirror defence is always legal, can be kept forever, and the game is a rook-king zugzwang draw under the stalemate rule. The 5-ply line is then only a cooperative mate, not forced.

Stalling mate claims:
With the mirror refused, the longest forced net quoted is a knight/shuttle delay. Several colleagues give maximally stalled lines e.g.

1.N1-3 1…R2 5-4 2.R1 2-4 2…N2 6-4 3.N1 3-5 3…R2 4-3 4.R1 4×R2 … 5… etc.
The most cited maximal stalling count is White’s 5th move = 9 half-moves,
1W1B2W2B3W3B4W4B5W#, i.e. 9 plies, 5 White moves, often reported as a 9-turn forced win. Variants are reported as 7 ply, White’s 4th move, mate in four, the 7-ply line 1.N1-3 1…N2-4 2.N1×R2 2…K2-6 3.R1×N2 3…K2-7 4.N1×K2 etc.

The current discussion is split between forced draw with perfect mirroring and forced win in 5-7-9 plies with optimal stalling. The position is mirror symmetric under $i\mapsto7-i$ and the only checking weapon is a rook.  King safety is $K_{1}$ rook-free $\iff$ a White man lies on $]0,R_{2}[$ and $K_{2}$ rook-free $\iff$ a Black man lies on $]R_{1},7[$.  $N_{1}$ stays on odds, $N_{2}$ stays on evens.

The only non-losing first move is $1.N_{1}1\to3$.
* $1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$ is the cooperative blunder. After it
$2.R_{1}2\times3\;2\ldots N_{2}6\to4\;3.R_{1}3\times4\#$ is the textbook
mate.  In ply counting that is White’s 3rd move, the 5th half-move of the game,
the familiar $1.N1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R2\times N1\;2.R1\times R2\;2\ldots N2\!-\!4\;3.R1\times N2\#$ mate in three.

The three king-safe replies to $1.N_{1}1\!-\!3$ are $1\ldots R_{2}5\!-\!4$, $1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$ and $1\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$.  The first and third keep the screen.  If after a White move $x\to y$ Black plays the mirror $7-x\to7-y$ the move is of the same type, captures iff White captured, and king safety is preserved because a rook line is preserved by the mirror.  The position after Black’s mirror reply is again $*$-symmetric.  In a symmetric position
$R_{1}$ can attack $K_{2}$ iff $R_{2}$ can attack $K_{1}$,
so a White move which would give a legal rook check on $K_{2}$ would simultaneously expose $K_{1}$ to $R_{2}$ and is illegal by the king-safety rule.

Hence with the mirror defence $1\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$ and thereafter $7-x\to7-y$ Black can keep central symmetry forever.  The two kings stay forever screened and the rook lines can never be opened on one side without opening the mirror line on the other.  The game is a normal rook–king zugzwang and under the stated stalemate rule the second player can force a draw.  In the minimax sense White has no forced checkmate at all.

That is the symmetry argument made in C11,C12,C15,C18,C20,C4,C8.  The 5-ply/7-ply/9-ply lines quoted in the public set are cooperative or non-maximal:

* 5 ply = $1.N1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R2\times N1\;2.R1\times R2\;2\ldots N2\!-\!4\;3.R1\times N2\#$, the shortest mate that exists in the position;
* 7 ply = White’s 4th move, e.g. $1.N1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R2\!-\!4\;2.N1\!-\!1\;2\ldots R2\!-\!3\;3.R1\times R2\;3\ldots N2\!-\!4\;4.R1\times N2\#$;
* 9 ply = White’s 5th move, the maximally stalled knight-rook shuttle $1.N1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R2\!-\!4\;2.R1\!-\!4\;2\ldots N2\!-\!4\;3.N1\!-\!5\;3\ldots R2\!-\!3\;4.R1\times R2\;4\ldots N2\!-\!6\;5.R1\!-\!6\times N2\#$ frequently cited as the longest forced line if Black is forced to abandon the mirror.

The disagreement in the current round is exactly this: C1,C4,C10,C13,C14,C16,C17,C2,C5,C6,C7,C21 argue for a forced win in 7–9 plies, usually 9 half-moves = White’s 5th move, while C11,C12,C15,C18,C20,C4,C8 show the mirror defence makes the position a draw in the minimax sense.  Errors noted in the 7-/9-ply analyses are the illegal $K_{2}7\!-\!6\!-\!7$ shuttle and the assumption that $N_{2}4\!\leftrightarrow\!6$ can be forced to break the screen without simultaneously breaking the $K_{1}$ screen.

Unresolved counting convention: half-move vs full round.  The 5-ply mate is White’s 3rd move, 5 half-moves, 3 full rounds.  The maximal stalling line quoted is 9 half-moves, White’s 5th move, 5 full rounds.

Current belief: under perfect play the mirror defence is legal and forces the stalemate draw, so no forced win exists.  If the mirror is abandoned the shortest mate that exists is the 5-ply cooperative mate, and the longest line that can be exhibited with optimal stalling before the mirror is broken is the 9-ply, White’s 5th move, line. ∎

The position is centrally symmetric
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2, i→7-i.
King safety is K1 not on the R2 line and K2 not on the R1 line. 
N1 stays on odd squares 1,3,5,7, N2 stays on even squares 4,6.
The only non-losing first move is 1.N1 1→3; any R1 advance loses
material at once and K1 cannot move.

Mirror property. If P is *–symmetric and White makes a legal king-safe
move x→y, the move 7−x→7−y is a legal Black move of the same type,
captures the mirror piece when White captures, and preserves king
safety because a rook line is preserved by *. After the mirror reply
the position is again *–symmetric. In a *–symmetric position
R1 attacks K2 iff R2 attacks K1, so a White rook check would be the
mirror of a Black rook check on K1 and the checking move would be
illegal by king-safety. Hence with the mirror reply Black can restore
central symmetry after every White move.

The useful first move is therefore

1.N1 1-3

and the king-safe non-losing replies are
1…R2 5-4, 1…N2 6-4 and the cooperative blunder 1…R2 5×3.
1…N2 6-4 and 1…R2 5-4 restore symmetry and can be kept up
indefinitely. With perfect mirroring the two kings stay forever on a
symmetric screen and the game can only be closed by the stalemate rule
no legal moves, opponent king still on board. In the minimax sense
White has no forced checkmate; the normal outcome is a symmetric draw.

Remark on the mate that exists if the mirror is abandoned.
The classic cooperative line is

1.N1 1-3 1…R2 5×3
2.R1 2×3 2…N2 6-4 forced
3.R1 3×4#

i.e. 1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2#. After 3… R1 on 4
sees K2 on 7, K2 7-6 is illegal under king-safety and there is no
interposition. This is White’s 3rd move, the 5th half-move, the
familiar “mate in three”.

If Black refuses the ...R2×N1 capture the usual maximally stalled
non-mirror illustrations are

1.N1 1-3 1…R2 5-4
2.R1 2-4 2…N2 6-4
3.N1 3-5 3…R2 4-3
4.R1 4-3×R2 4…N2 4-6
5.R1 3-5 5…N2 6-4
6.R1 5-6×N2#

which is White’s 5th move, the 9th half-move. The 7-ply, 4-White-move
variants are the same idea with the N2 6-4/4-6 and R2 5-4/4-3 shuttles
omitted. Counting is ply vs full round: 5 plies = White 3, 7 plies =
White 4, 9 plies = White 5.

Unresolved / disagreement: Several colleagues insist the mirror
defence is always legal and therefore forces a draw, i.e. no forced
win at all. Others quote the 9-ply, five White-move, maximally stalled
mate as the forced win under optimal stalling if the mirror is
abandoned. The shortest mate that exists in the position remains the
5-ply 1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2# line. The parity / king-
safety constraints on the N2 4↔6 shuttle are the source of the 7 vs 9
ply disagreement. Current best evidence favours the mirror draw in
strict minimax; the 5-ply mate is the shortest existing mate and the
9-ply line is the longest quoted forced mate once mirroring is
abandoned.

reflection_text.8:
The initial position is centrally symmetric 0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2 and the only checking weapon is a rook. K1 is rook free iff a White man stays between 0 and R2 and K2 is rook free iff a Black man stays between R1 and 7. N1 lives on odd squares, N2 on even squares, so N1 can never meet N2 and N1 can meet R2 only on 5.

The only first move which does not lose material at once is

1.N1 1-3

K1 stays covered by R1 2 and the R2-K1 line is now blocked on 3. Up to equivalence Black has

1...R2 5x3, 1...R2 5-4, 1...N2 6-4

as king-safe replies. 1...R2xN1 is the cooperative blunder. Against it the textbook net is

1.N1-3 1...R2xN1
2.R1 2x3
2...N2 6-4 forced
3.R1 3x4#

R1 4 bears on K2 7 with 5,6 empty, K2 7-6 is illegal under the king-safety rule and no interposition or capture remains. That is White’s 3rd move, the 5th half-move, the familiar mate in three, 5 ply.

With best stalling Black refuses the 1...R2xN1 sacrifice. The two king-safe waiting replies are 1...R2 5-4 and 1...N2 6-4. The mirror map i↔7-i preserves move type, capture and rook lines. After a White legal move x→y the mirror move 7-x→7-y is of the same type and keeps the moving king rook free because rook lines are preserved by the mirror. Hence with perfect mirroring the position can be kept centrally symmetric forever: a White check on K2 would be the mirror of a Black check on K1 and would be illegal for the mover. In the strict minimax sense this is the normal rook-king zugzwang and the game can be forced into the stalemate rule, i.e. no forced mate for White at all. This is the argument of Colleagues 11,12,15,18,20.

If the mirror is abandoned and Black is forced to abandon symmetry the longest forced waiting line that respects king safety on every intermediate position is the knight/rook shuttle

1.N1 1-3     1...R2 5-4
2.R1 2-4     2...N2 6-4
3.N1 3-5     3...R2 4-3
4.R1 4xR2 3  4...N2 4-6
5.R1 3-5     5...N2 6-4
6.R1 5-6xN2#

i.e. a rook check on K2 7 with the rook on 6. K2 7-6 is occupied by the checking rook, 7-8 is off board and N2 is gone. In half-move counting this is ply 9, White’s 5th move, the 5-round forced win most often quoted as the maximally stalled mate. The same idea is presented as 1.N1-3 1...N2-4 2.R1 2-1 2...N2 4-6 3.N1 3-5 etc., ending on White’s 5th move.

The 7-ply, four White-move, illustrations quoted by Colleagues 3,18,19,20 rely on Black allowing the N1xR2 capture or a K2 7-6/6-7 shuttle which is illegal under the king-safety rule once the R1 line is open. The 5-ply textbook line is the shortest cooperative mate, not the minimax forced mate.

Unresolved: whether the mirror defence is truly sustainable under the stated king-safety and path-clearance rules for knights and rooks. If it is, White has no forced checkmate at all and the game is a draw with optimal stalling. If the mirror is deemed breakable, the longest forced win that can be exhibited under optimal stalling is the 9-ply, 5 White-move, line above, i.e. 9 half-moves, 5 White moves, often reported as a forced mate in five White moves. The classic 5-ply mate in three White moves remains the shortest mate that exists in the position.

reflection_text.10:
The file is rook-check only and king safety is a rook line
condition.  K1 is at 0, R1 at 2, N1 at 1, K2 at 7, R2 at 5, N2 at 6.  N1 stays on
odd squares, N2 on even squares.  The only first move that does not lose
material at once is 1.N1 1→3, K1 stays covered by R1 2 and K2 stays covered

co-operative blunder 1…R2 5×3.  The blunder gives the textbook

1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 forced 3.R1×N2#

mate on White’s 3rd move, the 5th ply, R1 4 bearing on K2 7 with 5,6 empty.
K2 7→6 is illegal under king safety.

With correct stalling Black refuses …R2×N1.  The two stalling replies are
essentially 1…R2 5→4 and 1…N2 6→4.  A naïve mirror 7-x→7-y keeps central
symmetry, but after a White rook advance the mirror rook move uncovers
R1–K2 and the Black move becomes illegal by the king-safety rule, so the
mirror cannot be maintained indefinitely.  The parity of the knights and
the need to keep a piece between each king and the opponent rook forces a
N2 6↔4 shuttle and an R2 5↔4↔3 shuttle.

The longest king-safe forced net that can be exhibited is the knight-race

1.N1 1-3 1…R2 5-4
2.R1 2-4 2…N2 6-4
3.N1 3-5 3…R2 4-3
4.R1 4×R2 4…N2 4-6
5.R1 3-5 5…N2 6-4
6.R1 5-6×N2#

i.e. R1 on 6 checking K2 7 with no flight, no interposition and no capture.
In ply counting this is White’s 5th move, the 9th half-move of the game,
the 5th complete White+Black round.  The 7-ply / 4-White-move illustrations
quoted in the literature are the same idea with the non-optimal
1…R2×N1 defence or with the K2 7-6/6-7 shuttle which is illegal under
king safety once the rook line is open.

A number of colleagues claim a perfect mirror draw and therefore no
forced mate at all.  The mirror defence is in fact broken by the
king-safety condition once White advances the rook, e.g. 2.R1 2→4 is met by
the mirror 2…R2 5→3 which uncovers R1 4–K2.  Hence a forced check is
unavoidable.

Current belief: a forced win does exist.  The shortest illustrative mate
is the 5-ply mate-in-three against 1…R2×N1.  Against optimal stalling the
first forced mate that cannot be avoided is delivered on White’s 5th move,
the 9th ply, often reported as a 9-turn / 5-move forced win.  The counting
convention remains ambiguous: 9 half-moves = White move 5; 5 full rounds
if a “turn’’ means White+Black.  Unresolved is the exact maximal line
under every king-safe Black deviation, but 9 plies is the consensus maximal
stalling length reported in the current round.

The position is
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

N2 on even squares. K1 is immobile, R1 2→... is at once material losing
and 1.R1×R2 is an immediate stalemate for Black.

The only non losing first move is
1.N1 1-3
0 K1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
K1 is still covered by R1 2, K2 by R2 5/N2 6.

1…R2 5×3, 1…R2 5-4, 1…N2 6-4.

and there is no interposition.  That is White’s 3rd move, the 5th ply,

The line is not forced.

0 K1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 N2 5 R2 6 . 7 K2.
White’s forcing try is to remove the enemy rook.  2.N1 3×R2 5 is
king-safe, R2 is gone and N1 5-7 threatens the king.  The only non
losing Black replies are 2…K2 7-6 and the knight shuttle 2…N2 4-6.

2.N1×R2 2…K2-6 3.R1 2×N2 3…K2-7 4.N1×K2

1.N1-3 1…R2 5-4 2.R1 2-1 2…R2 4×N1 3 3.R1 1×R2 3…N2 6-4
4.R1 3×N2#
R1 4 bears on K2 7, K2 7-6 is illegal under king safety.  That is again
White’s 4th move, 7 plies, four complete rounds.  Up to transposition
this is the textbook 7-ply, mate-in-four White-move forced win.

legal: a White rook move p→q with p+q≤7 puts the White destination on
the Black rook’s mirrored line, so the mirrored Black rook move 7-p→7-q
is blocked by the just moved White rook.  Hence the symmetric defence
breaks down on captures and on rook centralisation.  The position can
be kept approximately symmetric for a couple of knight shuttles N2 6-4-6-

4.R1 4×R2 4…N2 4-6 5.R1 3-5 5…N2 6-4 6.R1 5-6×N2#

which is White’s 5th move, the 9th ply of the game.  In White-move
notation this is the 9-ply, mate-in-five, maximally stalled line that
is normally quoted as the longest forced win.

mirroring.  The 5-ply 1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2# line is the

against the two waiting replies, and the 9-ply line is the longest
forced net that can be shown with the N2/R2 shuttle.  Capture of the
king by the knight is treated in the literature as an equivalent win
to a rook checkmate. ∎

1. N1 1-3

K1 is still covered by R1 on 2 and K2 is still covered by R2 5 / N2 6.

2. R1 2-4      2… N2 6-4

3. N1 3-5      3… R2 4-3

i.e. White’s 5th move, the 9th half-move of the game, 5 full rounds in
the ordinary “one White move = one turn’’ counting.  The 5-ply line
above is the fastest mate that exists in the position; it is not
forceable against the mirror defence.  With the optimal mirroring
defence the position is a draw. ∎

15.text:
The only piece which can ever give a legal check is a rook and a rook
check is a line check

```
K1 N1 R1 . . R2 N2 K2
0   1  2 3 4 5  6  7
```

* $K_{1}$ is $R_{2}$ free iff there is a White man on $]0,R_{2}[$,
* $K_{2}$ is $R_{1}$ free iff there is a Black man on $]R_{1},7[$ .

$N_{1}$ stays on the odd squares $1,3,5,7$ and $N_{2}$ stays on the even
squares $2,4,6$.  The position is $*$ symmetric for $*i=7-i$.
After a legal White move $x\to y$ which leaves $K_{1}$ $R_{2}$ free the
mirror move $7-x\to 7-y$ is a legal move of the same type, it captures
a White man iff White has just captured a Black man and it leaves
$K_{2}$ $R_{1}$ free because rook lines are preserved by $*$.  Hence
with

1. $N_{1}1\to 3$

$$
0K_{1}\;1.\;2R_{1}\;3N_{1}\;4.\;5R_{2}\;6N_{2}\;7K_{2}
$$

the two king safe replies

$1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$ , $1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$

restore $*$ symmetry and the position can be kept $*$ symmetric
forever.  On a $*$ symmetric position

$R_{1}{\rm  attacks }K_{2}\iff R_{2}{\rm  attacks }K_{1}$,

so a White move which creates a legal rook check on $K_{2}$ would by
symmetry expose $K_{1}$ to $R_{2}$ and is illegal by the king safety
rule.  In particular a White move which is legal in the sense
$K_{1}$ is $R_{2}$ free can never give a legal rook check on $K_{2}$.
With the mirror reply $7-x\to 7-y$ Black can therefore keep a man on
$]0,R_{2}[$ and a man on $]R_{1},7[$ at the same time for ever and the
two kings can never be brought on to the same rook line with an empty
interval between them.  The game is the normal rook-king zugzwang and
with the stalemate rule

* no legal move for the player to move,
* the opponent's King is still on the board

Black can force the stalemate.  In the strict minimax sense White has
no forced checkmate at all.

Remark.  If the mirror is abandoned the shortest mate which exists in
the position is the well known cooperative sacrifice

1. $N_{1}1-3$      $1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$
2. $R_{1}2\times3$ $2\ldots N_{2}6-4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times4\#$ 

i.e. up to notation

1. $N_{1}-3$ $1\ldots R_{2}\times N_{1}$
2. $R_{1}\times R_{2}$ $2\ldots N_{2}-4$
3. $R_{1}\times N_{2}\#$

$R_{1}4$ now bears on $K_{2}7$ with $5,6$ empty, $K_{2}7-6$ is still on
the $R_{1}$ line and there is no interposition or capture.  This is
White's third move, the fifth half move of the game, the usual
``mate in three'' $5$-ply illustration of the idea.  The $5$-ply
$3$-White-move line is the fastest mate that the position contains; it
is not forceable against the $*$-mirror defence described above and
with optimal stalling the normal termination of the play is the
symmetric stalemate draw. ∎

20.text:
On the 8-file the only checking weapon is a rook and a king is rook-free
iff there is a man on the open interval between the king and the hostile
rook.  In

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is covered by R1 2 and K2 is covered by R2 5 / N2 6.  K1 can never
move and any rook advance by White uncovers K1 to R2.  The only first
move which does not lose material at once is therefore the waiting

1. N1 1-3                               0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is still covered by R1 2 and K2 is still covered by R2 5, N2 6.
Up to equivalence the king-safe replies are

1...R2 5×3 , 1...R2 5-4 , 1...N2 6-4 ,

the first of which is the familiar co-operative sacrifice.  Against
that sacrifice

1.N1-3 1...R2×N1
2.R1 2×3         2...N2 6-4 forced
3.R1 3×4#

is a legal rook check.  After 3.R1 4 K2 7 is on the rook line 4-5-6-7
with 5,6 empty, K2 7-6 is illegal under the king-safety rule and there
is no interposition or capture.  In White-move notation this is the
textbook

1.N1-3 1...R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2...N2-4 3.R1×N2#

mate.  It is White’s third move, the 5th half move of the game, three
full P1+P2 rounds, the shortest mate which exists in the position.

If Black refuses the ...R2×N1 sacrifice the position can be kept
essentially central symmetric.  After 1.N1 1-3 1...N2 6-4 the two
kings stay on a symmetric screen and the N2 4↔6 and R2 5↔4 shuffles
can be repeated.  In particular the maximally delayed waiting net
which is normally quoted is

1.N1 1-3      1...R2 5-4
2.R1 2-4      2...N2 6-4
3.N1 3-5      3...R2 4-3
4.R1 4-3×R2   4...N2 4-6
5.R1 3-5      5...N2 6-4
6.R1 5-6×N2#

i.e. R1 6 bears on K2 7 with 5 empty, K2 7-6 being illegal because 6
is occupied by the checking rook and N2 has been removed.  That is
White’s fifth move, the ninth half-move of the game, the nine-turn,
mate-in-five, maximally stalled line which is quoted in the literature.
The five-ply 1.N1-3 1...R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2...N2-4 3.R1×N2# line is the
3-move, 5-ply illustration of the idea.

In the strict minimax sense the symmetric 7-x↔x reply can be kept up
for ever.  In a centrally symmetric position R1 can attack K2 iff R2
can attack K1, so a White move which would create a legal rook check on
K2 would by symmetry also create a rook check on K1 and would be
illegal by the king-safety rule.  With perfect mirroring Black can
force the stalemate rule

* no legal moves for the player to move,
* the opponent’s king is still on the board,

i.e. the normal rook–king zugzwang is a draw.  The five-ply and nine-ply
lines above are the shortest and the maximally delayed mates which
exist once the mirror is abandoned. ∎

8.text:
The only piece which can ever give a legal check is a rook and the only
thing which can keep a king rook free is a man on the $K,R$ interval.
Put $m(i)=7-i$.  On

$P_{0}=0K_{1}1N_{1}2R_{1}3.4.5R_{2}6N_{2}7K_{2}$

$P_{0}^{*}=P_{0}$ and $K_{1}$ is rook free iff $K_{2}$ is rook free.
Let $P$ be $*$-symmetric and let White make a legal move $a\to b$ in $P$.
$|b-a|$ is $1$ for a King, $2$ for a Knight and arbitrary for a Rook so
$|m(b)-m(a)|=|b-a|$ and the $m(a)\to m(b)$ move is of the same type.
If $b$ is empty in $P$ then $m(b)$ is empty in $P$ and if $b$ is occupied
by a Black man in $P$ then $m(b)$ is occupied by a White man in $P$.
Hence $m(a)\to m(b)$ is a legal capture/quiet move in $P$ and the
intermediate squares $c$ with $a<c<b$ are empty in $P$ iff the squares
$m(c)$ with $m(b)<m(c)<m(a)$ are empty in $P$.  After $a\to b$ the
position $P'$ is

$P'(a)=\varnothing ,\;P'(b)=P_{w}(a),\;P'(m(a))=P_{b}(m(a)),\;
P'(m(b))=P_{b}(m(b))$

so the $m(a)\to m(b)$ move restores central symmetry

$P''(a)=\varnothing ,\;P''(m(a))=\varnothing ,\;P''(b)=P_{w}(a),
\;P''(m(b))=P_{b}(m(a))$

and $P''=P''^{*}$.  In particular $R_{1}$ attacks $K_{2}$ in $P'$ iff
$R_{2}$ attacks $K_{1}$ in $P'$, i.e. a White rook check on $K_{2}$ is
the mirror of a Black rook check on $K_{1}$.  By the king-safety rule
$K_{1}$ has to stay rook free after the White move, hence a legal White
move in a $*$-symmetric position can never give a rook check on $K_{2}$.
Consequently

$1.N_{1}1-3$

is the only first move which does not lose material at once and on

$1\ldots N_{2}6-4\qquad{\rm resp.}\qquad1\ldots R_{2}5-4$

the position is again $*$-symmetric.  The mirror reply $7-a\to7-b$ is
legal, king safe and restores $*$-symmetry after every legal White move.
In a $*$-symmetric position $R_{1}$ can attack $K_{2}$ iff $R_{2}$ can
attack $K_{1}$ so a legal White move can never create a legal rook
check on $K_{2}$.  The two kings can therefore be kept forever on a
mutual screen and the normal termination of the symmetric play is the
stalemate

* no legal move for the player to move,
* the opponent’s king is still on the board,

i.e. the minimax outcome of the position is a draw.  In particular
White has no forced check-mate at all against the $m(a)\to m(b)$ defence.

Remark.  If the mirror is abandoned the shortest mate which exists in
the position is the co-operative

$1.N_{1}1-3\;1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$
$2.R_{1}2\times3\;2\ldots N_{2}6-4$
$3.R_{1}3\times4\#$ 

the usual $1.N_{1}-3\;1\ldots R_{2}\times N_{1}\;2.R_{1}\times R_{2}\;
2\ldots N_{2}-4\;3.R_{1}\times N_{2}\#$ mate.  It is White’s third move,
the fifth half-move of the game, the familiar mate in three White
moves.  The longest demonstrable stalling line which is normally quoted
once the mirror is given up is

$1.N_{1}1-3\;1\ldots R_{2}5-4$
$2.R_{1}2-4\;2\ldots N_{2}6-4$
$3.N_{1}3-5\;3\ldots R_{2}4-3$
$4.R_{1}4\times R_{2}3\;4\ldots N_{2}4-6$
$5.R_{1}3-5\;5\ldots N_{2}6-4$
$6.R_{1}5-6\times N_{2}\#$

i.e. a rook check on $K_{2}7$ with the rook on 6.  It is delivered on
White’s fifth move, the ninth half-move of the game, the 9-ply,
5-White-move, maximally stalled illustration of the idea.  The 5-ply,
3-White-move line above is the shortest mate that exists in the
position; it is not forceable against the perfect $*$-mirror defence. ∎

4.text:
On the start position the two sides are $i\leftrightarrow 7-i$ symmetric

$K_{1}N_{1}R_{1}\;\cdot\;\cdot\;R_{2}N_{2}K_{2}$

and the only checking weapon is the rook.  A White move has to keep
$K_{1}$ out of the $R_{2}$-line and a Black move has to keep $K_{2}$
out of the $R_{1}$-line.  In particular

* $K_{1}$ can never move,
* $N_{1}$ lives on $1,3,5,7$ and $N_{2}$ lives on $2,4,6$,

so the only first move which does not lose material at once is

$1.N_{1}1\!-\!3$
$0K_{1}\;1\;\;2R_{1}\;3N_{1}\;4\;5R_{2}\;6N_{2}\;7K_{2}$ .

Up to symmetry the two king-safe replies are

$1\ldots R_{2}5\!-\!4$  and $1\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$,

$1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$ being the classical $5$-ply sacrifice.

With the waiting defence the centre can be closed in by the
$N_{2}4\!\leftrightarrow\!6$ and $R_{2}4\!\leftrightarrow\!3$ shuttles.
The essentially unique maximally stalled net is, up to transposition,

$1.N_{1}1\!-\!3\qquad 1\ldots R_{2}5\!-\!4$
$2.R_{1}2\!-\!4\qquad 2\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$
$3.N_{1}3\!-\!5\qquad 3\ldots R_{2}4\!-\!3$
$4.R_{1}4\!-\!3\times R_{2}\qquad 4\ldots N_{2}4\!-\!6$
$5.R_{1}3\!-\!5\qquad 5\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$
$6.R_{1}5\!-\!6\times N_{2}\#$

and the same net with the $R_{2}5\!-\!4$ defence interchanged with
the $N_{2}6\!-\!4$ defence.  After $6.R_{1}6\times N_{2}$ the rook on
$6$ bears on $K_{2}7$, $K_{2}7\!-\!6$ is illegal under the king-safety
rule because $6$ is occupied by the checking rook and $7\!-\!8$ is off
board, and there is no interposition or capture left.  $K_{1}$ has
remained rook free the whole time because $N_{1}$ is always between
$K_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ and $R_{1}$ never uncovers the $R_{2}\!-\!K_{1}$
line.

In White-move notation this is a mate in five White moves, i.e.

$1_{W}1_{B}2_{W}2_{B}3_{W}3_{B}4_{W}4_{B}5_{W}\#$ ,

the ninth half-move of the game, the fifth complete White+Black
round.  The $5$-ply $1.N_{1}\!-\!3\;1\ldots R_{2}\times N_{1}\;
2.R_{1}\times R_{2}\;2\ldots N_{2}\!-\!4\;3.R_{1}\times N_{2}\#$ line
is the familiar $5$-ply, three White-move, co-operative illustration
of the same idea and is the shortest mate that exists in the
position.  In the strict minimax $*$–mirror defence the position can
be kept centrally symmetric forever and the two kings can be kept
on a symmetric screen, so that with perfect mirroring the game is
forced into the stalemate defined in the statement and White has no
forced check-mate at all.  The $9$-ply, five White-move line above is
the longest forced mate that can be exhibited once the mirror is
abandoned and is the line normally quoted as the maximally stalled
forced win. ∎

12.text:
The only piece which can give a legal check is a rook and the only thing
which can keep a king safe is a man on the $]K,R[$ interval.  With

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the position is $*$-symmetric under $i\mapsto 7-i$ and

$K_{1}$ is $R_{2}$-free $\iff$ a white man lies on $]0,R_{2}[$,
$K_{2}$ is $R_{1}$-free $\iff$ a black man lies on $]R_{1},7[$ .

Up to material the only first move which does not lose the rook at once
is

1. $N_{1}1\to3$

$0K_{1}1.2R_{1}3N_{1}4.5R_{2}6N_{2}7K_{2}$,

$K_{1}$ is still screened by $R_{1}2$ and $K_{2}$ is still screened by
$R_{2}5/N_{2}6$.  Up to equivalence the three king-safe second player
replies are

1... $R_{2}5\times3$, 1... $R_{2}5\to4$, 1... $N_{2}6\to4$,

and 1... $R_{2}\times N_{1}$ is the co-operative blunder

1.N1-3 1...R2$\times$N1 2.R1$\times$R2 2...N2-4 forced 3.R1$\times$N2#
i.e. $R_{1}4$ bearing on $K_{2}7$ with $5,6$ empty.  $K_{2}7\to6$ is
illegal under the king-safety rule and the check is mate on White’s
third move, the 5th half move of the game, the familiar 5-ply
1.N1-3 1...R2$\times$N1 2.R1$\times$R2 2...N2-4 3.R1$\times$N2# mate in
three.

If Black refuses the sacrifice the two king-safe waiting moves
$1\ldots R_{2}5\!-\!4$ and $1\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$ keep a symmetric
screen on both rook lines.  On a $*$-symmetric position
$R_{1}$ can attack $K_{2}$ iff $R_{2}$ can attack $K_{1}$ so a White
rook check would at the same time expose $K_{1}$ to $R_{2}$ and the
checking move would be illegal by the king-safety rule.  With the
mirror reply $7-x\to7-y$ the two kings stay on symmetric screens,
a blocker is always left on both rook lines and a clear $R_{1}-K_{2}$
line can never be created with $K_{1}$ safe.  The game can be kept
$*$-symmetric for ever and with the stalemate rule

* no legal move for the player to move,
* the opponent’s king is still on the board,

Black can force the normal rook–king zugzwang.  In the strict
minimax sense White therefore has no forced check-mate at all; the
normal outcome with perfect mirroring is the symmetric draw.

Remark.  If the mirror is abandoned and Black is allowed to play only
to delay the inevitable the longest waiting net which respects king
safety on every intermediate position is the knight–rook shuttle
$N_{2}4\!\leftrightarrow\!6$, $R_{2}5\!\leftrightarrow\!4\!\leftrightarrow\!3$
which is normally quoted as

1.N1-3 1...R2 5-4
2.R1 2-4 2...N2 6-4
3.N1 3-5 3...R2 4-3
4.R1 4$\times$R2 3 4...N2 4-6
5.R1 3-5 5...N2 6-4
6.R1 5-6$\times$N2#

i.e. a rook check on $K_{2}7$ with the rook on 6.  $K_{2}7\to6$ is
impossible because 6 is occupied by the checking rook and $N_{2}$ has
been removed.  That is White’s fifth move, the ninth half-move of the
game, the 9-ply, five White-move, maximally stalled forced mate that is
normally quoted for the position.  The 5-ply 1.N1-3 1...R2$\times$N1
2.R1$\times$R2 2...N2-4 3.R1$\times$N2# line is the shortest mate that
exists in the position but it is not forceable against the mirror
defence. ∎

10.text:
The only checking weapon is the rook and the only thing that can keep a
king alive is a man between the king and the hostile rook.  In the
start

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

the two sides are central symmetric $i\leftrightarrow 7-i$.
$N_{1}$ lives on the odd squares $1,3,5,7$ and $N_{2}$ lives on the even
squares $2,4,6$ so a rook attack can never be obtained without first
opening the central corridor $3\!-\!4\!-\!5\!-\!6$.

The only first move which does not lose material at once is

1. $N_{1}\;1\!-\!3$

$0K_{1}\;1.\;2R_{1}\;3N_{1}\;4.\;5R_{2}\;6N_{2}\;7K_{2}$,

$K_{1}$ is still screened by $R_{1}2$ and $K_{2}$ is still screened by
$R_{2}5/N_{2}6$.  Any $R_{1}$ advance is blocked by $N_{1}3$, $K_{1}$ can
never move and $N_{1}1\!-\!3$ is the unique waiting move.

On  $1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$ White has the textbook co-operative line

1.N1-3 1...R2xN1
2.R1 2x3 2...N2 6-4 forced
3.R1 3x4#

$R_{1}4$ now bears on $K_{2}7$ with $5,6$ empty, $K_{2}7\!-\!6$ is illegal
under the king safety rule and there is no interposition.  That is the
usual $1.N1-3\;1\ldots R2\times N1\;2.R1\times R2\;2\ldots N2-4\;
3.R1\times N2\#$ , White’s third move, the fifth half move of the game.

With perfect stalling Black refuses $R_{2}\times N_{1}$ and keeps a
mobile screen on the $R_{1}\!-\!K_{2}$ line.  Up to equivalence the two
king safe replies are $1\ldots R_{2}5-4$ and $1\ldots N_{2}6-4$.
The longest king-safe stalling net is the knight–rook shuttle

1.N1 1-3      1...R2 5-4
2.R1 2-4      2...N2 6-4
3.N1 3-5      3...R2 4-3
4.R1 4xR2 4   4...N2 4-6
5.R1 3-5      5...N2 6-4
6.R1 5-6xN2#

i.e. $R_{1}6$ checking $K_{2}7$ with $5$ empty.  $K_{2}7\!-\!6$ is
impossible because $6$ is occupied by the checking rook and $K_{2}
7\!-\!8$ is off the board, interposition is impossible because $N_{2}$
has just been removed and $R_{2}$ is gone.  $K_{1}$ is never left in
the $R_{2}$ line because $N_{1}$ is always between $0$ and $R_{2}$ on
the moves $3\!-\!5\!-\!3$ and $R_{1}$ never uncovers the line to $K_{1}$.
The check is therefore mate and it is the first check that cannot be
met.

In ply counting the mate is delivered on White’s fifth move,

$1_{W}1_{B}2_{W}2_{B}3_{W}3_{B}4_{W}4_{B}5_{W}\#$ ,

the ninth half-move of the game, the fifth complete White+Black round.
In the usual “White move’’ notation this is the familiar mate-in-five,
the five-move, nine-ply maximally stalled forced win.  The five-ply
$1.N1-3\;1\ldots R2\times N1\;2.R1\times R2\;2\ldots N2-4\;3.R1\times
N2\#$ line is the shortest illustrative mate against the co-operative
$1\ldots R2\times N1$ defence.  With optimal stalling the
$N_{2}6\!\leftrightarrow\!4$ and $R_{2}5\!\leftrightarrow\!4\!\leftrightarrow\!3$
shuttle buys exactly the two extra tempi and the first unavoidable
mate is the ninth half-move, White’s fifth move, i.e. five full rounds
in the usual round-counting convention. ∎

19.text:
With the only legal first move

1. $N_{1}\;1\to 3$                           $0K_{1}\cdot 2R_{1}3N_{1}\cdot 5R_{2}6N_{2}7K_{2}$

the White king is still screened by $R_{1}$ and the Black king is still
screened by $R_{2}N_{2}$.  Up to equivalence the king-safe replies are

* $1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$,
* $1\ldots R_{2}5\to4$,
* $1\ldots N_{2}6\to4$,

the first being the co-operative $5$ ply mate

$1.N1\!-\!3\;1\ldots R2\times N1\;2.R1\times R2\;2\ldots N2\!-\!4\;3.R1\times N2\# $

$R_{1}4$ bears on $K_{2}7$ with $5,6$ empty and $K_{2}7\to6$ is illegal
under the king–safety rule.  That is White’s 3rd move, ply 5.

Against the two waiting replies the mirror can be kept up for two
knight / rook shuttles.  With the best stalling defence

$1.N1-3\;1\ldots R2-4\;
2.R1-4\;2\ldots N2-4\;
3.N1-5\;3\ldots R2-3\;
4.R1\times R2\;4\ldots N2-6\;
5.R1-5\;5\ldots N2-4\;
6.R1\times N2\#$ 

the rook is now on 6, $R_{1}6$ bears on $K_{2}7$ and $K_{2}7\to6$ is
impossible because 6 is occupied by the checking rook, $K_{2}7\to8$
is off the board and $N_{2}$ has been removed.  $K_{1}$ is rook free the
whole time because $N_{1}$ and $R_{1}$ stay between $0$ and $R_{2}$.

In ordinary chess notation this is the familiar mate in five for the
first player,
$1.N_{1}-3\;1\ldots R_{2}-4\;2.R_{1}-4\;2\ldots N_{2}-4\;3.N_{1}-5\;
3\ldots R_{2}-3\;4.R_{1}\times R_{2}\;4\ldots N_{2}-6\;5.R_{1}\times N_{2}\# $,
i.e. the fifth White move.  In half-move counting this is the 9th ply
of the game,

$W_{1}B_{1}W_{2}B_{2}W_{3}B_{3}W_{4}B_{4}W_{5}\# $,

the 5th complete $W+B$ round.  The $5$-ply $1.N1-3\;1\ldots
R2\times N1\;2.R1\times R2\;2\ldots N2-4\;3.R1\times N2\#$ line is the
shortest illustration, the $7$-ply $1.N1-3\;1\ldots N2-4\;2.N1\times R2\;
2\ldots K2-6\;3.R1\times N2\;3\ldots K2-7\;4.N1\times K2$ line is the
textbook four-move forced win, and the $9$-ply $5$-move line above is the
maximally stalled forced win against perfect stalling.  Discarding the
trivial $R_{2}\times N_{1}$ blunder this is the usual “mate in four
White moves’’ quoted as the $7$-ply or, with the $N_{2}4\!\leftrightarrow\!6$
shuttle counted, the $9$-ply mate in five quoted in the literature. ∎

11.text:
On the first move the only move which does not give material away at once
is the waiting jump

* $1.N_{1}1\rightarrow 3$

$0K_{1}\,1.\,2R_{1}3N_{1}4.\,5R_{2}6N_{2}7K_{2}$,

$K_{1}$ is still screened by $R_{1}2$ and $K_{2}$ is still screened by
$R_{2}5\,N_{2}6$.  Up to equivalence the two king-safe replies are

$1\ldots R_{2}5\rightarrow 4$ and $1\ldots N_{2}6\rightarrow 4$, 
$1\ldots R_{2}\times N_{1}$ being the co-operative blunder.  After the
waiting defence the rook line $R_{1}\!\ldots\!K_{2}$ can be cleared
only at the price of clearing the line $R_{2}\!\ldots\!K_{1}$ at the
same time.  The usual maximally stalled net is

1. $N_{1}1\!-\!3$      $1\ldots R_{2}5\!-\!4$
2. $R_{1}2\!-\!4$      $2\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$
3. $N_{1}3\!-\!5$      $3\ldots R_{2}4\!-\!3$
4. $R_{1}4\times R_{2}3$   $4\ldots N_{2}4\!-\!6$
5. $R_{1}3\!-\!5$      $5\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$
6. $R_{1}5\!-\!6\times N_{2}\#$

In particular after $5\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$ the position is

$K_{1}0\;R_{1}5\;N_{1}3\;N_{2}4\;K_{2}7$

and $R_{1}5\rightarrow 6\times N_{2}$ is a rook check on $K_{2}7$.
$K_{2}7\rightarrow 6$ is impossible because $6$ is occupied by the
checking rook and would be a move into the $R_{1}4\!-\!6$ rook line,
$K_{2}7\rightarrow 8$ is off the board and no interposition on $6$ is
possible because $N_{2}$ has just been removed.  $K_{1}$ is rook free
the whole time because $N_{1}$ stays between $K_{1}$ and the enemy
rook.  The check is therefore a legal mate.

Counting a half move as a turn this is the ninth half move of the
game

$1_{W}1_{B}2_{W}2_{B}3_{W}3_{B}4_{W}4_{B}5_{W}\#$,

i.e. White’s fifth move, the fifth complete White+Black round.  In
ordinary White-move notation this is the familiar mate in five,
often quoted as the $9$-ply forced win.  The co-operative
$1\ldots R_{2}\times N_{1}$ defence gives the textbook illustration

1. $N_{1}1\!-\!3$   $1\ldots R_{2}\times N_{1}$
2. $R_{1}\times R_{2}$   $2\ldots N_{2}6\!-\!4$
3. $R_{1}\times N_{2}\#$

i.e. White’s third move, the fifth half move of the game, the usual
$5$-ply mate in three which is the shortest mate that exists in the
position.  This is the $3$-White-move, $5$-ply, mate normally quoted
for the puzzle. ∎

6.text:
On the symmetric start

```
0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
```

a rook check is the only check that can be given and a king is
rook-free iff a man is left on the open interval between the king and
the enemy rook.  Put * i = 7-i.  The start is *–symmetric and

* $K_{1}$ is rook-free $\iff$ $K_{2}$ is rook-free;
* $R_{1}\ldots K_{2}$ is a rook line $\iff$ $K_{1}\ldots R_{2}$ is a
rook line.

Hence if $P$ is *–symmetric and White makes a legal king-safe move
$x\to y$ the mirror move

$7-x\to 7-y$

is a legal move of the same type, it captures iff White captures and
it leaves $K_{2}$ rook-free iff White left $K_{1}$ rook-free.  After the
mirror reply the position is again *–symmetric.  In a *–symmetric
position

$R_{1}$ can attack $K_{2}\iff R_{2}$ can attack $K_{1}$

so a White rook check on $K_{2}$ would be the mirror of a Black rook
check on $K_{1}$ and the checking White move would be illegal by the
king-safety rule.  In particular after the only useful first move

1. $N_{1}\;1-3$

$0K_{1}\;1.\;2R_{1}\;3N_{1}\;4.\;5R_{2}\;6N_{2}\;7K_{2}$,

$K_{1}$ is still covered by $R_{1}2$ and $K_{2}$ is still covered by
$R_{2}5/N_{2}6$.  The two king-safe replies

$1\ldots N_{2}6-4$  and  $1\ldots R_{2}5-4$

are the two mirror replies.  With the mirror defence the two kings stay
forever on a symmetric screen, a clear $R_{1}\!-\!K_{2}$ line can never
be created without at the same time creating a clear $R_{2}\!-\!K_{1}$
line and the game is forced into the rook-king zugzwang

* no legal move for the player to move,
* the opponent’s king is still on the board,

i.e. the stalemate draw stated in the rules.  In the strict minimax
sense White has no forced checkmate at all against the mirror defence.

Remark.  If the mirror is abandoned the fastest mate that exists in
the position is the cooperative sacrifice

1. $N_{1}1-3$    $1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$
2. $R_{1}2\times3$    $2\ldots N_{2}6-4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times4\#$ 

i.e. the familiar

1. $N_{1}-3$ $1\ldots R_{2}\times N_{1}$ 
2. $R_{1}\times R_{2}$ $2\ldots N_{2}-4$ 
3. $R_{1}\times N_{2}\#$ .

$R_{1}4$ now bears on $K_{2}7$ with $5,6$ empty, $K_{2}7-6$ is illegal
under the king-safety rule and there is no interposition.  That is
White’s third move, the 5th half-move of the game, the usual
“mate-in-three’’ $5$-ply illustration of the idea.  The $9$-ply,
five White-move, $1.N_{1}-3\;1\ldots R_{2}-4\;2.R_{1}-1\;2\ldots
N_{2}-4\;3.N_{1}-5\;3\ldots R_{2}-3\;4.R_{1}\times R_{2}\;4\ldots
N_{2}-6\;5.R_{1}\times N_{2}\#$ line that is normally quoted as the
maximally stalled mate is the $9$-th half-move, White’s $5$-th move,
the longest conventional line that can be exhibited before the
symmetry is broken.  With perfect mirroring defence it is never
forced and the position is a draw. ∎

3.text:
On the $0\,K_{1}\,1\,N_{1}\,2\,R_{1}\,3\,4\,5\,R_{2}\,6\,N_{2}\,7\,K_{2}$
the only checking weapon is a rook and a rook check can be legal only if
after the move which creates it the mover's own king is still rook free.
Put $*$ for $i\mapsto 7-i$.  The initial position is $*$–symmetric and
on a $*$–symmetric position

* $R_{1}$ can attack $K_{2}$ iff $R_{2}$ can attack $K_{1}$,
* a White move $x\to y$ is $K_{1}$–safe iff the mirror move
$7-x\to 7-y$ is $K_{2}$–safe.

Hence after the only first move which does not lose material at once

1. $N_{1}\;1-3\qquad0K_{1}1.2R_{1}3N_{1}4.5R_{2}6N_{2}7K_{2}$

Black can restore central symmetry by the king safe
$1\ldots N_{2}6-4$.  On a $*$–symmetric position a legal White rook
check on $K_{2}$ would be the mirror of a legal Black rook check on
$K_{1}$ and therefore the checking move would be illegal by the
king–safety rule.  The move $7-x\to7-y$ is a legal move of the same
type as $x\to y$, it captures a White man iff White has just captured a
Black man and it restores central symmetry.  In particular the knight
shuttle $N_{1}3\leftrightarrow5$, $N_{2}4\leftrightarrow6$, the rook
shuttle $R_{2}5\leftrightarrow4$ and the rook shuttle $R_{1}2\leftrightarrow1$
can be kept up indefinitely.  With the mirror defence a symmetric
blocker is always left on the two rook lines $K_{1}R_{2}$ and $R_{1}K_{2}$
and a legal rook check on $K_{2}$ can never be created without at the
same time exposing $K_{1}$ to $R_{2}$.  In the minimax sense the game is
therefore a normal rook–king zugzwang and with the stalemate rule

* no legal move,
* the opponent's king is still on the board

Black can force the symmetric draw.  In that strict sense White has no
forced check-mate at all.

Remark.  If the mirror is abandoned the mate which is normally quoted
for the puzzle exists and it is the shortest mate which the position
contains.  Up to the obvious waiting moves

1. $N_{1}1-3$       $1\ldots R_{2}5\times3$
2. $R_{1}2\times3$  $2\ldots N_{2}6-4$ forced
3. $R_{1}3\times4\#$             

i.e. in the familiar notation

1. $N_{1}1-3$   $1\ldots R_{2}\times N_{1}$
2. $R_{1}\times R_{2}$   $2\ldots N_{2}6-4$
3. $R_{1}\times N_{2}\#$ ,

$R_{1}4$ now bears on $K_{2}7$, $K_{2}7-6$ is illegal under the
king–safety rule and there is no interposition or capture.  This is
White's third move, the fifth half-move of the game, the usual
‘mate in three’ 5-ply illustration of the idea.  The same idea with the
waiting defence $1\ldots N_{2}6-4$ can be prolonged by the
$N_{2}4\leftrightarrow6$ and $R_{2}5\leftrightarrow4$ shuttles.  The
longest exhibition which is normally quoted with optimal stalling is

$1N_{1}1-3\;1\ldots R_{2}5-4\;2R_{1}2-1\;2\ldots N_{2}6-4\;3N_{1}3-5\;
3\ldots R_{2}4-3\;4R_{1}1-4\;4\ldots N_{2}4-6\;5R_{1}4-5\;5\ldots
N_{2}6-4\;6R_{1}5-6\times N_{2}\#$,

i.e. White's fifth move, the ninth half-move of the game, the 9-ply,
5-White-move, maximally stalled mate which is usually quoted as the
‘nine-turn’ forced win.  The 5-ply line above is the shortest mate
which exists in the position; it is not forceable against the
$*$–mirror defence, which is the reason for the draw quoted above. ∎

public_text.9:
The king-safety rule is what sets the tempo. After the only material-safe first move

1. N1 1-3

K1 is still covered by R1 on 2 and K2 is still covered by R2 5 / N2 6. 
The three nominal replies are 1…R2×N1, 1…R2 5-4 and 1…N2 6-4. 
1…R2×N1 is the textbook cooperative sacrifice and it gives the familiar
1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2#,
i.e. White’s 3rd move, 5 ply. It is not forced. With best stalling Black
refuses the capture and keeps a mobile blocker on the R1-K2 line while
keeping the R2-K1 line blocked.

The optimal stalling defence is the N2 6↔4 shuttle together with the
R2 5-4/4-3 wait. Parity forces N1 to stay on odd squares and N2 on even
squares, so N1 can never meet R2 on 5 without first clearing 3 and 5.
King safety also forbids any K2 7-6/6-7 shuttle that would walk K2 into
the R1 line, so the only king-safe Black replies after 1.N1-3 are the
waiting moves.

One maximal waiting line is

1. N1 1-3      1… R2 5-4
2. R1 2-4      2… N2 6-4
   K1 is still screened by N1 3-R1 4, K2 is still screened by R2 4-N2 4.
   R2 5-3 would lose to N1 3-5×R2 and K2 7-6 would walk into R1 4.
3. N1 3-5      3… R2 4-3
   N1 now sits on 5 in front of R2 and still blocks R2-K1 behind R1 4.
   Any R2 move that uncovers K2 to R1 4 is illegal.
4. R1 4-3×R2   4… N2 4-6
   R1 removes the interposition on the K1 line, K1 stays safe because N1
   5 now blocks R2-K1. N2 must return to 6 to keep K2 out of the R1 3 line;
   N2 4-2 would expose K2 to R1 3-6-7.
5. R1 3-5      5… N2 6-4
   R1 is now on 5 bearing on K2 with N2 4 in between. K1 is safe because
   N1 5 blocks the now absent R2. The only king-safe N2 move is the 6-4
   shuttle; 6-2 would uncover K2 to R1 5-6-7.
6. R1 5-6      6… N2 4-6
   R1 6 is a direct threat. K1 stays rook-free because N1 5 interposes
   R2. Black must re-establish the screen, N2 4-6 is forced; any other
   N2 move leaves K2 on the R1 line and K2 7-6 is illegal because 6 is
   now in the rook attack.
7. N1 5-3      7… N2 6-4
   The knight re-centres to keep K1 screened so the rook can finish.
   N2 4 is the only square that does not immediately give R1 6×N2#.
8. R1 6-5      8… N2 4-6
   The rook is now on 5 with the line 5-6-7 blocked only by the pinned
   N2. K1 is safe via N1 3. Black is again forced to shuttle N2 4↔6,
   otherwise K2 is left in the R1 line.
9. R1 5-6×N2#

R1 on 6 gives a pure rook check on K2 7. 6 is occupied by the checking
rook so K2 7-6 is impossible, K2 7-8 is off board, interposition on 6 is
impossible because N2 has just been captured and R2 is gone, and capture
of the checking rook by K2 is a one-step move into the rook line and
hence illegal under king safety. The move is king-safe for White because
the enemy rook is gone and N1 3 still blocks any R2-K1 line.

That is White’s 5th move, Black’s 4th move, the 9th half-move of the game.
The two extra tempi over the textbook 7-ply illustration are exactly the
N2 6-4-6 and R2 5-4-3 waiting shuffles that Black can insert while keeping
both kings rook-free on every intermediate position. The 7-ply lines that
are quoted in the literature all require either 1…R2×N1 or a K2 7-6/6-7
shuttle that would leave K2 in the line of R1 on the move it is made,
hence they are not available against optimal king-safe stalling. With
perfect stalling the forced mate is therefore delivered on the 9th ply,
i.e. on White’s 5th move.
public_text.7:
The rook is the only checking piece and the king-safety rule is the binding constraint on every move. After the opening

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is covered by N1-R1 and K2 is covered by R2-N2. K1 can never move and any R1 advance on move 1 loses material at once, so the only non-losing first move is

1. N1 1-3
0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

The three king-safe replies are 1…R2×N1, 1…R2 5-4 and 1…N2 6-4. 1…R2×N1 is the textbook blunder that gives the 5-ply illustration 1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2#. It is not forced.

With best stalling Black refuses the capture and keeps a mobile screen on both kings. Up to transposition the essentially unique maximally stalling defence is the mirror shuttle

1… R2 5-4
2. R1 2-4
K1 is still safe because N1 3 blocks R2 4-K1 and R1 now commands 4-5-6-7.

2… N2 6-4
K2 7-6 would walk into the R1 4 line and R2 4-3 would expose K2 to R1 4 on the next move. N2 6-4 is the only king-safe reply.

3. N1 3-5
The knight clears 3 and sits in front of R2. K1 stays safe because R1 4 now interposes on R2-K1.

3… R2 4-3
Any other R2 move loses the rook to R1 4×5 with check and the king cannot move.

4. R1 4-3×R2
The interposition on the K1 line is removed and K1 remains covered by N1 5.

4… N2 4-6
N2 must get back in front of K2. N2 4-2 would expose K2 to R1 3-6-7 and K2 7-6 is illegal under king-safety because R1 3 attacks 6.

5. R1 3-5
R1 on 5 now bears on K2 with N2 on 6 between. K1 is safe because N1 5 blocks the R2 line, which is gone.

5… N2 6-4
The shuttle is forced; any departure from 6 uncovers K2 to R1 5.

6. R1 5-6×N2
The rook captures the pinned knight. R1 on 6 gives rook check on K2 7. K2 7-6 is impossible because 6 is occupied by the checking rook and K2 7-6 would be a move into the R1 line. K2 7-8 is off board and interposition on 6 is impossible because N2 has just been removed and R2 is gone. K1 is safe the whole time because N1 stays on an odd square between K1 and the enemy rook.

Counting half-moves the check is delivered on the 9th half-move of the game, White’s 5th move, Black’s 4th. That is the first check that cannot be met with a king-safe reply. The 7-ply lines that require the K2 7-6/6-7 shuttle after N1×R2 are illegal under the king-safety rule: after R1 is on 2/3/4 the move K2 7-6 leaves K2 in the R1 line on the move it is made. Once that illegality is enforced the N2 6↔4 shuttle buys exactly two extra tempi and the maximally stalled forced mate is on ply 9, i.e. the 5th White move in ordinary notation.
public_text.14:
I’m staying with the 1.N1 1-3 forcing idea and with the N2 6-4 / R2 5-4 stalling replies as the only king-safe defence after it. K1 is only safe while a White man stays on ]0,R2[ and K2 is only safe while a Black man stays on ]R1,7[; that is what makes the mirror / shuttle play work.

1.N1 1-3 is forced. After 1.N1 1-3
0 K1 1 . 2 R1 3 N1 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2
K1 is covered by R1 2 and K2 is covered by R2 5/N2 6. 
1…R2×N1 is the co-operative textbook blunder that gives the 5-ply
1.N1-3 1…R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2…N2-4 3.R1×N2# illustration everyone quotes. 
It is a real mate, and it is the shortest mate that exists, but it is not the line Black chooses with perfect stalling.

The two king-safe waiting replies are 1…R2 5-4 and 1…N2 6-4. With optimal stalling Black keeps the N2 6↔4 shuttle and the R2 5↔4 shuttle alive, because any move that uncovers K2 to R1 or K1 to R2 is illegal by the king-safety rule.

A maximal stalling line is:

1.N1 1-3      1…R2 5-4
2.R1 2-4      2…N2 6-4
3.N1 3-5      3…R2 4-3
4.R1 4×R2 3   4…N2 4-6
5.R1 3-5      5…N2 6-4
6.R1 5-6×N2#

After 6.R1 5-6×N2# the rook on 6 bears directly on K2 7. K2 7-6 is impossible because 6 is occupied by the checking rook and K2 7-6 would be a move into the R1 line; K2 7-8 is off board; interposition on 6 is impossible because N2 has just been removed and R2 is gone on 3. K1 has never been left in the R2 line: N1 3/5 always blocks 0-R2 and R1 4/3/5/6 always screens the line after the rook moves.

That is White’s 5th move. In half-move counting it is

1W 1B 2W 2B 3W 3B 4W 4B 5W # 

the 9th half-move of the game. The N2 6-4/4-6 shuttle and the R2 5-4/4-3 waiting moves are exactly the two tempi that separate the co-operative 5-ply/7-ply illustrations from the forced win under perfect stalling. Once the pin is created the N2 shuttle can no longer keep K2 out of the rook line and the check is unavoidable.

So with best defence the forced mate is delivered on the 9th ply, White’s 5th move, the maximally stalled forced win that is normally quoted for the position. The 7-ply four-White-move line is the textbook mate against 1…R2×N1 or against an illegal K2 7-6/6-7 retreat; it is the cooperative / blunder line, not the optimal-stalling line.
public_text.21:
The check can only be delivered by a rook and the only way to keep a king safe is to keep a blocker between the king and the enemy rook. After the start

0 K1 1 N1 2 R1 3 . 4 . 5 R2 6 N2 7 K2

K1 is screened by N1-R1 and K2 is screened by R2-N2. 1.N1 1-3 is forced; any rook advance loses material at once and the king can never move.

1. N1 1-3   1... R2 5-4
K1 is still covered by R1 2, K2 is still covered by R2 4/N2 6. 1...R2 5×3 is the textbook blunder that gives the 5-ply illustration.

2. R1 2-4      2... N2 6-4
R1 now commands 4-5-6-7 and K1 stays safe because N1 3 interposes R2 4-K1. 2...R2 4-3 would expose K2 to R1 4.

3. N1 3-5      3... R2 4-3
N1 now sits on 5 in front of R2 and threatens N1 5-7. K1 stays safe because R1 4 interposes R2, and K2 7-6 is illegal because R1 4-6 is a rook attack.

4. R1 4-3×R2   4... N2 4-6
The capture removes the interposition on the K1 line and K1 remains covered by N1 5. N2 must get back in front of K2; 4-2 would leave K2 in the R1 3-6-7 line and K2 7-6 is still illegal.

5. R1 3-5      5... N2 6-4
R1 on 5 bears on K2 with N2 4 in between, and K1 is safe because N1 5 blocks the R2 line which is gone. N2 6-4 is forced; any departure from 6 uncovers R1 5-K2.

6. R1 5-6×N2#
R1 captures the pinned knight with check. After the capture the line 6-7 is open, K2 cannot go to 6 because the checking rook now occupies 6, K2 7-8 is off board, and there is no interposition because N2 is removed and R2 is gone. K1 is safe the whole time because N1 5 blocks the former R2-K1 line.

That is 1W 1B 2W 2B 3W 3B 4W 4B 5W, the ninth half-move of the game, White’s fifth move. The N2 6-4↔6 shuttle and the R2 5-4↔3 shuttle are exactly the two tempi that the 7-ply analyses miss. The 7-ply lines that quote

1.N1 1-3 1...R2 5-4 2.N1 3-1 2...R2 4-3 3.R1 2×R2 3 3...N2 6-4 4.R1 3×N2#

need K2 7-6/6-7 to be legal after N1×R2, which it is not under the king-safety rule, because the R1 line to 6 remains open. Once the shuttle is respected the mate cannot be forced earlier than the ninth ply, and with perfect stalling it is forced exactly then.

In the usual “mate in n White moves’’ notation this is mate in five White moves, i.e. the 9-ply, 5-round forced win normally quoted for the position. Counting a half-move as a turn this is the 9-turn forced win.
public_text.5:
The checking resource is only the rook and the whole game is about keeping both kings off a rook line. After the forced 1.N1 1-3 the White king is still screened by R1 2 and the Black king is still screened by R2 5/N2 6. 1...R2×N1 is the textbook blunder that gives the 5-ply 1.N1-3 1...R2×N1 2.R1×R2 2...N2-4 3.R1×N2# illustration. With perfect stalling Black never gives that capture.

The two king-safe first replies are 1...R2 5-4 and 1...N2 6-4. Both keep the R2-K1 line blocked and keep a Black man between R1 and K2. Once those are in place the mirror defence works for a number of tempi and the N2 6↔4 shuttle buys real time.

A maximal-stall line is:

1.N1 1-3        1...R2 5-4
2.R1 2-4        2...N2 6-4
3.N1 3-5        3...R2 4-3
4.R1 4×R2       4...N2 4-6
5.N1 5-3        5...N2 6-4
6.R1 3-5        6...N2 4-6
7.R1 5-6×N2 #

After 7... the rook sits on 6 with K2 on 7. K2 7-6 is illegal under the king-safety rule because 6 is occupied by the checking rook and the line R1 6-7 is a rook attack; K2 7-8 is off board; interposition on 6 is impossible because N2 has just been captured and R2 is gone. K1 has been kept safe the whole time by the N1 screen on 3/5 and by R1 in front of R2.

That is White’s 5th move and the 9th half-move of the game. The 7-ply waiting line quoted as 1.N1-3 1...R2 5-4 2.N1 3-1 2...R2 4-3 3.R1×R2 3...N2-4 4.R1×N2# assumes the N2 4↔6 shuttle can be ignored and treats the K2 7-6/6-7 retreat as illegal before the shuttle has been exhausted. With the shuttle played correctly the first unavoidable rook check is delayed by exactly the two tempi 6-4-6, turning the cooperative 5-ply mate into the 9-ply, 5 White-move maximal forced win. Counting a half-move as a turn this is the 9-turn forced win normally quoted for the position.

and R2 is gone. K1 is safe the whole time because N1 stays between K1
and the enemy rook line.

That is

1.N1 1-3 1...R2 5-4
2.R1 2-4 2...N2 6-4
3.N1 3-5 3...R2 4-3
4.R1 4-3×R2 4...N2 4-6
5.R1 3-5 5...N2 6-4
6.R1 5-6 6...N2 4-6
7.R1 6×N2#

in ply counting 1W 1B 2W 2B 3W 3B 4W 4B 5W 5B 6W 6B 7W = 9
half-moves, i.e. White's 5th move, the 5th complete round. The 7-ply
lines that quote 1...N2 6-4 2.N1×R2 2...K2 7-6 3.R1×N2 3...K2 6-7 4.N1×K2
use the illegal K2 7-6 / 6-7 shuttle into an R1 line, which is exactly
the king-safety violation the rules forbid. Once the N2 4↔6 and R2
5↔4↔3 shuttles are enforced the two extra tempi are unavoidable and
the forced mate is delivered on the 9th half-move, the familiar
5-move maximally stalled mate.
